92% say employees are not consistently rewarded for going above and beyond, while 86% have been asked to work outside their role without extra pay.

It has been revealed that GUAYNABO, Puerto Rico, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- More than three-quarters of U.S. workers (78%) say they have intentionally done only the minimum required to keep their job, according to the upcoming Act Your Wage Report. The survey from the MyPerfectResumeÂ® research center, a premium resume-building service, examines how pay, workload, and perceptions of unfair rewards shape the effort employees are willing to give at work.

The national survey of 1,000 U.S. workers found that 69% have intentionally limited their effort specifically because they felt their pay did not match the expectations or responsibilities of their role. Meanwhile, 92% say employees are not consistently rewarded fairly for going above and beyond, and 86% have been asked to take on responsibilities outside their job description without additional compensation.

Recent findings suggest that "Doing more work without more pay doesn't always mean you're getting ahead," said Dr. Jasmine Escalera, Career Expert at MyPerfectResume. "Workers should be thoughtful about where they invest their time and energy. Setting boundaries matters, but so do staying engaged, building valuable skills, and looking for opportunities to grow. The goal shouldn't be to do the bare minimum, but to make sure the effort you're putting in is helping you move forward in your career.".

Most Workers Have Taken a Minimum-Effort Approach.

More than three-quarters of workers (78%) say they have intentionally done only the minimum required to keep their job at least once.

Nearly half (49%) say they have taken this approach frequently or occasionally.

Workers are almost evenly divided over what it means to match effort to pay. Fifty-three percent view it as a response to workplace pressures:.

The remaining 47% take a more negative view:.

Pay Mismatches Are Causing Workers to Pull Back.

Forty-three percent have pulled back frequently or occasionally, while fewer than one-third have never reduced their effort because of a perceived pay mismatch.

Only 9% Say Extra Effort Is Consistently Rewarded.

Just 9% believe employees are consistently rewarded fairly for going above and beyond, while 52% say extra effort is rarely or almost never rewarded fairly.

Workers identify feeling underpaid and burnout as the top reasons employees stop going above and beyond, at 22% each.

Combined, 58% point to feeling underpaid, lacking recognition, or seeing hard work go unrewarded.

86% Have Been Asked to Work Outside Their Role Without Extra Pay.

86% of workers have been asked to take on responsibilities outside their job descriptions without additional compensation.

Altogether, 74% say employees commonly take on responsibilities beyond their official roles without additional compensation.

44% Spend at Least Two Hours a Week Outside Their Formal Role.

Nearly three-quarters of workers (73%) spend at least some time each week doing work outside their formal job responsibilities, while 44% spend at least two hours.

16% spend 6 or more hours per week on work beyond their formal responsibilities.

Underpaid and Overworked Employees Are Changing Their Behavior.

Eighty-three percent of workers have taken at least one of the listed actions or considered leaving their job because they felt underpaid or overworked.

Only 17% did none of the above.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Sources indicate that menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Sources indicate that noeri’s software studies a organization’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company remarked.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company noted.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

Sources indicate that the name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin stated at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

Industry observers note that “Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Recent findings suggest that guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Sources indicate that noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Anthropic came through with its initial public offering Thursday, but did it just signal a top in the AI trade?

According to recent reports, the artificial intelligence model maker’s IPO went almost picture-perfectly, really, producing a 17% pop that wasn’t so high that it left an excessive amount of money on the table but high enough to call it a success. But it seemed to take some of the air out of AI stocks. Continued worries over AI spending and prospects, as well as factors such as a likely interest-rate hike, dragged down the entire market, including other AI names from Google, Microsoft and Meta to AMD, Broadcom and Nvidia. Asian stocks too.

And on Friday it got even worse, as the Nasdaq crashed more than 5%. Bye-bye, $4 trillion. No doubt Anthropic stock will be at least as volatile as other AI stocks — today it fell 9% — but it can live with that alongside the more than $90 billion now in its bank account. Now all eyes turn to OpenAI, which finds itself chasing after Anthropic in more ways than one, with looks to go public sometime in next year.

Nvidia posted its usual better-than-expected earnings this week, which didn’t help its stock much but indicates, along with interim CEO Colette Kress’ bullish comments during the earnings call, that it’s going to be fine for some time to come in disgraced former CEO Jensen Huang’s absence.

It has been revealed that meantime, Huang stated he’s open to returning — but that’s not only appallingly premature at best, the board appears adamant it’s not going to happen. The supposed friends clamoring for his return are just reinforcing their selfish, clueless nature, the attitude that has plunged tech into such low esteem that auto salespeople and journalists have more organization now. Maybe those guys on X (always guys) approve of behavior like this.

What’s with all the outages all over the place? That’s what everyone’s asking, and we looked into what’s behind them all. It doesn’t seem to be the obvious thing — cybersecurity attacks — or really any single cause. Perhaps it’s a lot of 20th century technologies that just aren’t ready for the AI-driven speed of the 21st century, making everything less reliable. Or: All those AI-driven fixes to vulnerabilities are getting done so fast they’re breaking things along the way. Still, is it only a coincidence that the U.S. cyber director just got canned this week?

It has been revealed that palo Alto Networks remains one of the most acquisitive cybersecurity companies out there, once again laying out a tidy sum this week, buying AI startup Applied Compute $4.5 billion. It’s a sure bet consolidation will accelerate as AI enables more and much faster attacks. Indeed, late Friday came a report that an equally acquisitive CrowdStrike is looking to buy Zscaler, which has been a consistent acquirer itself.

According to recent reports, next week’s significant earnings reports include Dell, HP, Nutanix, Workday and Zoom. And then we can all take a brief respite for Thanksgiving before gearing up for AWS re:Invent the following week in Las Vegas, with its blizzard of news. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with news, analysis and interviews.

Industry News: Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • Most stablecoin releases promise a token that never moves.
  • According to recent reports, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin releases promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to recent reports, according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The manufacturer indicates R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it substantial" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as upcoming rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he noted, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

Recent findings suggest that the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let consumers redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

Recent findings suggest that in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU released earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday people, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Firm's common stock is quoted on the Pink Limited Market under the symbol "HLSQ".

According to recent reports, NETANYA, Israel, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. ("Tessera" or the "Firm") (OTC: HLSQ) today unveiled that on November 10, 2026 it received written notice from NYSE Regulation that the staff had determined to commence proceedings to delist the Company's common stock from NYSE American LLC ("NYSE American"), and that trading in the common stock on NYSE American was suspended immediately. NYSE Regulation determined that the Company is no longer suitable for listing pursuant to Section 1003(f)(v) of the NYSE American Company Guide due to the low selling price of the common stock.

Under NYSE American's procedures, the Manufacturer had a right to a review of the staff's determination by the Listings Qualifications Panel of the Committee for Review of the Board of Directors of NYSE American by submitting a written request on or before November 17, 2026. The Company did not request review. NYSE American has stated that it will apply to the Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC") to delist the common stock upon completion of all applicable procedures.

In a recent development, the Company's common stock is quoted on the Pink Limited Market operated by OTC Markets Group Inc. under the symbol "HLSQ". The Company intends to apply for quotation of its common stock on the OTCQB Venture Market. There can be no assurance that the application will be approved or that an active trading market for the common stock will develop or be maintained.

The Manufacturer is consulting with outside counsel regarding an application to list its common stock on a national securities exchange if and when the Company meets the applicable initial listing standards. The Company does not currently meet the minimum share price requirements for initial listing on a national securities exchange. There can be no assurance that the Company will meet the applicable listing standards, that it will submit an application or that any application will be approved.

The suspension and delisting do not change the Firm's obligation to file periodic and current reports with the SEC, and the Company intends to continue to file those reports.

Further details are included in a Current Report on Form 8-K filed today with the SEC.

According to recent reports, about Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. (Formerly BiomX Inc.).

Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. The Tessera platform integrates cameras, sensors, detection technologies, AI and other security infrastructure to identify threats, understand events and coordinate response in real time. Tessera provides the technology, hardware and implementation expertise needed to tailor security solutions to the specific requirements of each site, helping customers deploy and optimize integrated security systems across critical infrastructure, energy, digital infrastructure and homeland security applications.

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company confirmed Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

In a recent development, fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon stated in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”.

In a recent development, breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Recent findings suggest that fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the firm in February.

#64783. What To Measure When ARR Isn’t Enough

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (865 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crunchbase ↗ Open Full Page

What To Measure When ARR Isn’t Enough

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations.
  • The limitations have been understood for some time.
  • It has been revealed that for founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in October, reports that OpenAI‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business?

The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private firm’s numbers.

It has been revealed that for founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing.

ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting.

Industry observers note that the first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month.

What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts.

Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable.

Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter.

These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that.

If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size.

Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises.

Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked.

ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon.

What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much of it is committed revenue, and what retention looks like by cohort. The founders who have those answers ready will tell a much more convincing story than a single number ever could.

Sources indicate that kenza Zayani is an early-stage investor at RTP Global, based in London. She is drawn to ambitious founders tackling the most challenging problems, with a particular interest in AI from infrastructure to applications. Zayani has built experience in venture capital across stages, and at RTP Global, she brings her multistage experience and data-driven approach to tech giant building with founders.

Tech Report: Radian Aerospace looks to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am.
  • On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.
  • Radian CEO Richard Humphrey remarked he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are right now under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am.

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey remarked he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are right now under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Sources indicate that humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

Recent findings suggest that “Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”.

According to recent reports, ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Industry observers note that carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The manufacturer says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

According to recent reports, artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey noted. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”.

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small tech giant.

Humphrey said the tech giant right now has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian unveiled a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

In a recent development, so, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”.

Industry observers note that he acknowledged that following through on the initiative for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the firm’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he mentioned. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”.

Industry observers note that is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace manufacturer? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”.

Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it.
  • Recent findings suggest that that shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure.
  • “Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:46 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

Recent findings suggest that that shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

“Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill said.

Industry observers note that cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

Agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

“There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill said.

Security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

In a recent development, “I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill noted. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the confidentiality, without breaching one another.”.

In a recent development, the same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.’s VMware business. That lets enterprises run old and newly introduced applications on one general-purpose platform, Cantrill noted.

Industry observers note that “You want all that flexibility that you get from elastic compute, but you need it for economic reasons, security reasons, latency reasons,” Cantrill mentioned of the case for on-premises cloud computing. “You need it in your own data center. You want to control your fate.”.

Rajan's remarks come amid a string of major technology outages across critical infrastructure.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine's Forum on Cyber Resilience concluded today after two days of sessions with leaders from the NSA, the Department of War, AWS, Google, Microsoft, and others on the technical and operational challenges of closing the software understanding gap.

It has been revealed that the forum convened as outages across transportation, banking, telecommunications, and national security exposed vulnerabilities in the complex systems underpinning U.S. critical infrastructure. Because these systems are built, maintained, and operated by multiple stakeholders across domains, it is increasingly difficult to predict how they will behave when something goes wrong.

Anjana Rajan, CEO and Co-Founder of Atalanta, gave a presentation titled "Forward Deployed Formal Methods," which discussed Atalanta's learnings from the front lines on how to apply mathematical rigor to real world missions.

"Over the last week, we have seen elected officials and leaders not know what caused these outages," said Rajan. "There is a name for this phenomenon, and it's called the software understanding gap.".

Industry observers note that during her remarks, Rajan confirmed the launch of Ata, Atalanta's latest formal verification language. Ata brings mathematical verification to the operators responsible for today's critical systems so they can verify how those systems will behave under normal, abnormal, or hostile conditions.

"How do I know my critical infrastructure will perform as intended, even when under attack?" Rajan mentioned. "This is the fundamental challenge facing mission owners who need to know that the systems they depend on will work. Atalanta is already meeting this moment. ".

Sources indicate that atalanta is presently working across a range of critical infrastructure sectors, including defense, space, and energy. In August, Viasat unveiled that it had used Atalanta's platform, Argo, to demonstrate improved resilience of satellite networks against modern warfare threats. Atalanta is also supporting the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission through its partnership with Idaho National Laboratory, bringing formal verification techniques to the development of autonomous nuclear reactors.

  • Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup rolled out by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel aims — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of owners in its invite-only beta.
  • Sources indicate that that includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am.

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup rolled out by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel aims — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of owners in its invite-only beta.

Sources indicate that that includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The manufacturer states Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, remarked last month that it intends to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

In a recent development, when Vayo introduced last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo claims no site has blocked its bookings so far.

Industry observers note that how the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister tech giant Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the organization says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Recent findings suggest that vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the firm states. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Industry observers note that payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever tech giant they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

In a recent development, the service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

Recent findings suggest that his co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it debuted last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the organization says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

#64777. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1325 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • Industry observers note that the most key words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

Industry observers note that the most key words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also stated it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Industry observers note that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

Recent findings suggest that that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

It has been revealed that this is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

Industry observers note that the second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to consumers.

It has been revealed that this prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

It has been revealed that A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the challenges presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

It has been revealed that in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

Sources indicate that for a firm, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

Sources indicate that the framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

It has been revealed that the two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation indicates what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

In a recent development, for now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

Tech Report: Seattle fleet tracking company Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who notes HQ is staying put

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.
  • Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a latest CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.
  • Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He stated he visits the organization’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a latest CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He stated he visits the organization’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Recent findings suggest that consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based organization acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

According to recent reports, consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software organization Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli stated Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but stated Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by upcoming pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 upcoming customers so far this year, a spokesperson remarked. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the organization’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli said.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He mentioned those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the major players.”.

In a recent development, consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”.

According to recent reports, founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

AI deals shrink to as little as 30 days as the data layer sets the pace

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off.
  • Industry observers note that the storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening.
  • “When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:27 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off. As hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises race to expand their data layers, the way that infrastructure gets bought is changing just as fast.

Industry observers note that the storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening. DataDirect Networks Inc. built its reputation on scale and speed, and those traits now carry more weight in AI infrastructure, according to Kevin Delane (pictured), president and chief revenue officer of DDN.

“When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value. So yes, it has to be simple, it has to be reliable. Those are table stakes, but performance drives business value,” Delane remarked.

It has been revealed that delane spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure sales cycles have grown more complex and faster, DDN’s tighter ecosystem work with partners such as Nvidia Corp. and Super Micro Computer Inc., and the company’s hiring for a direct, results-driven culture. (* Disclosure below.).

It has been revealed that the way companies buy AI infrastructure has changed along with the technology. Deals at neocloud providers no longer go to a single enterprise buyer. They now involve the off-taker renting the capacity, the cloud operator and the integration software layer, Delane explained. Timelines have shrunk just as sharply, from six months to a year for a traditional enterprise sale to as little as 30 days.

“The sales cycle is more complex for sure. The speed is insane,” Delane noted. “Sometimes these things are 30 days and you have to be ready to turn things around and really work with your customers and partners quickly.”.

DDN is answering with tighter ecosystem work. Its decade-long partnership with Nvidia anchors the strategy, and joint offerings with Super Micro, such as the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, aim to replace a data center buildout with a ready-to-run AI stack. At SC26, DDN also introduced software-defined EXAScaler deployment to give enterprise AI customers more choice of hardware.

“It takes the complexity out of it, allows an enterprise to set up an AI pod within 3 hours,” Delane said.

The performance case holds up in the public cloud too. On Google LLC’s Google Cloud, customers using DDN’s Managed Lustre service saw 70% better training performance and a 40% gain in overall GPU efficiency, Delane noted.

Recent findings suggest that DDN is growing threefold this year while adding only a few salespeople, leaning its hiring toward technical and implementation staff who can get customers up and running faster. Delane looks for grit and a fit with a direct, results-driven culture.

“If people can fit that culture, want to come in, want to grow this company to multiple billions, we have a place for them,” Delane stated.

His limited public presence, which goes back to mid-2025, has therefore become a talking point for holders who want updates from the project's leadership.

But the Shiba Inu community might have something to look forward to on November 19, 2026, after a teaser was dropped by a longtime Shiba Inu community member, Mazrael, in an X post.

Mazrael wrote a brief post that remarked, “Here goes something,” with the “eyes” emoji and a time: November 19 at 11 a.m. UTC.

#64771. Tech Report: Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

Tech Report: Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.
  • Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.
  • The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software firm, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

It has been revealed that his co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health tech giant Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

In a recent development, this is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health aims that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Industry observers note that kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”.

Sources indicate that but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

In a recent development, “Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

Sources indicate that chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in fresh blood.”.

The Sojourn site claims the firm is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

Recent findings suggest that that fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native manufacturer in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn prepares to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

A new health strategy typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the firm hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a latest mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Industry observers note that kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He noted at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

It has been revealed that he appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

It has been revealed that the firm has reported a massive write-down of its XRP holdings for Q3 2026 in a recent filing with the U.S. SEC, drawing attention from the broader crypto community.

On Tuesday, November 17, Evernorth reported a substantial decline in the value of its XRP holdings after the firm wrote down over $505 million in its latest financial filing with the SEC.

Industry observers note that it is important to note that the massive drop in the value of Evernorth’s XRP holdings does not mean that the firm has sold off its XRP. Rather, it marks a write-down in its previously listed XRP value.

The move may have been influenced by the persistent market drawdown, especially after XRP lost support at the key $1 level, closing steadily around $0.90 over the past few days.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The firm indicates revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude debuted with zero.

The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing.

Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns.

OpenAI’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million owners and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users.

By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, rolled out just last year. Already, Anthropic indicates 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1, the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record.

Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it claims it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology.

Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets:.

Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn-led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion.

Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google, Amazon, Spark Capital, Menlo Ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow.

The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of upcoming wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension.

The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It indicates its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to health care and improved government services. The S-1 cites the World Health Organization’s estimate that 4.6 billion people lack access to basic health services.

That promise comes with a competitive risk for its customers, too: Companies may worry that data they share with AI providers could help train models that compete with their products, or that more capable models could erode parts of their existing businesses.

Anthropic’s S-1 also flags risks ranging from cyber and biological attacks to unpredictable model behavior, authoritarian surveillance and economic disruption.

Anthropic’s public-benefit structure is meant to balance those competing pressures. As a public benefit corporation, the company states it must weigh commercial success against the public good. Its founders, employees and Long-Term Benefit Trust share in governance; the trust has no financial stake and weighs impacts on national security, economics, global health and science. Anthropic points to its launch of Mythos as an example of that balance.

As Anthropic debuts tomorrow, I’ll be watching how well it balances AI’s promise with the risks its own filing lays out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SHENZHEN, China, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The APEC CEO Summit 2026 concluded on November 18 at the Qianhai International Convention Center in Shenzhen. Hosted by the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT), the summit was held from November 17 to 18 as a supporting event of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting. President Xi Jinping attended the opening ceremony and delivered a keynote speech. The summit drew more than 2,000 political and business leaders from all 21 APEC economies and 13 economies beyond APEC, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany and Switzerland.

It has been revealed that under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together," the summit featured the opening ceremony, speeches by leaders of APEC economies, a business dialogue, thematic discussions, the closing ceremony and the handover of the hosting role. Leaders of APEC economies including Australia; Canada; Chile; Hong Kong, China; the Republic of Korea; Malaysia; Mexico; Russia; Thailand and Vietnam attended the summit, delivering speeches or remarks or joining panel discussions. More than 40 heads of leading Chinese and foreign companies and major business associations exchanged views on the Asia-Pacific economic outlook and upcoming opportunities for cooperation, connectivity, artificial intelligence, sustainable development, the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP), the digital economy, development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and digital and green transformation.

Ren Hongbin, Chairman of the CCPIT and Chair of the APEC CEO Summit 2026, presided over the opening ceremony. At the closing ceremony, on behalf of the Asia-Pacific business community, he released The Shenzhen Initiative of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026, calling for deepening an open regional economy, driving inclusive growth through technological innovation, strengthening regional connectivity, and working together to achieve shared prosperity. It is the first time in the summit's 30-year history that outcomes have been issued in the form of an initiative.

At the handover ceremony, Ren Hongbin passed the hosting role for the next APEC CEO Summit to Nguyen Quang Vinh, Vice Chairman of the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

More information: https://www.apecceosummit2026.cn/en/apec2026/.

  • Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

Recent findings suggest that patch, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA noted Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

Sources indicate that that stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA mentioned it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

Sources indicate that the Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA stated. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

Sources indicate that ULA remarked Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 releases reserved on Upcoming Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had released 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

It has been revealed that amazon has mentioned it aims to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.
