📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle tech giant talked about building for years but always found too major to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

Industry observers note that “The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” noted Joe Duffy, the manufacturer’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”.

According to recent reports, the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy stated there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The tech giant isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

According to recent reports, pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:.

According to recent reports, to decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy remarked he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

Sources indicate that “Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” remarked Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Sources indicate that both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise looks.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy noted.

Recent findings suggest that AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Sources indicate that duffy stated many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of manufacturer: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The upcoming products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he remarked.

Sources indicate that “This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy stated. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

It has been revealed that neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy remarked.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

It has been revealed that pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the manufacturer’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy remarked. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy stated Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the organization, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy mentioned, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

In a recent development, despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy mentioned Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy mentioned Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

I Used to Counteroffer My Best Employees With More Money. Now I Rely on These 3 Strategies.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving.
  • According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

According to recent reports, like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

According to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making. And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

Recent findings suggest that given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or company equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

I am not suggesting that it is wrong to counteroffer someone’s resignation with money. However, it’s reactive and arbitrary. Unless you have put a cap on how high you are willing to go, your negotiations will begin to feel like a moving target that’s out of your control. Again, you may end up delaying someone’s departure, but you won’t keep them forever unless you put more proactive measures in place.

Industry observers note that some positions in your organization drive enterprise value and some don’t. McKinsey and Company suggested in an older article that these will probably make up about 5% of your workforce — and contribute 800% more than others across your organization.

According to recent reports, over the years, I’ve found that I could typically name fewer than 10 roles that would materially impact my business if they remained vacant for an extended period. My recommendation is to name those roles and then create retention looks for each of them.

What are some focused plan ideas? Deferred compensation structures allow team members to grow their money tax-free as long as they stay with your organization. That way, you won’t inflate your overall payroll and can concentrate your resources where they matter most. This type of long-term incentive can be tangibly meaningful because it’s tied to tenure and not merely performance. Since it’s only applicable to a small group of high-value employees, you aren’t raising your compensation across your organization, either.

Industry observers note that I once considered using equity as a major retention lever. Why not? It felt right and seemed to be a no-brainer way to get people to stick around and contribute to our manufacturer’s growth. Yet when I mapped out the risks and rewards, I realized that giving away equity has massive long-term costs.

It has been revealed that here’s the issue: equity permanently dilutes your ability to use equity in other ways later. For example, you can’t bargain with equity with potential investors if a chunk of it has been given to your employees. Going the equity route also complicates your organizational governance, which can make your financial picture blurry.

Recent findings suggest that rather than offering equity to someone who wants to leave, explore non-equity alternatives. Treat equity as a last resort that you’ll only consider if you think it will bring out an employee’s long-term ownership behavior. And be open to talking about this with a professional who has helped other businesses design executive benefit and compensation structures that retain key people while protecting tax exposure and equity. Looking for a resource to get your feet wet? Colin Steinberg, a partner at Institutional Architects, frequently shares advice on executive planning and related topics.

Sources indicate that there are many business-friendlier alternatives to simply handing an employee who’s about to leave more money or equity. As mentioned before, you might provide deferred compensation, a way to delay income that benefits both you and the team member.

You might also look into supplemental executive retirement aims. Chances are strong that you already offer retirement benefits. Could you offer additional ones directly tied to both tenure and performance? Supplemental executive retirement plans help C-suite employees see meaningful future value in putting down roots, which SmartAsset explains can help trim churn among your highest-paid performers.

When structured appropriately, these types of retention strategies avoid immediate financial strain on your balance sheet. They also allow you to turn retention tools into ways to improve your tax efficiency, reduce volatile compensation models and retain control over your equity.

I firmly believe that founders who lose their most valuable people (but are otherwise building solid, fair companies) don’t have a problem with their retention. They have a problem with the way they’ve structured their long-term compensation packages for their most impactful roles. If you want to get real leverage as an employer, you need to develop smarter systems that incentivize your key players without losing your ground.

Like all business leaders, I have had some of my top performers tell me they were leaving. There is no way to sugarcoat the feeling. It’s like a kick in the belly — and in the wallet.

Industry observers note that according to statistics reported by HR Morning, replacing an employee costs upwards of 200% of what they were making. And that is probably a conservative figure, given that losing a valuable team member can cause a ripple of lowered productivity and tabled projects as people scramble to pick up the ex-employee’s work.

In a recent development, given these facts, I used to follow the standard pattern of attempting to keep talented team members by offering them higher compensation, bonuses or manufacturer equity. It was a tactic that almost always worked, but it didn’t create loyalty. Instead, it made those people price-sensitive, and they eventually found organizations willing to pay more, so they left anyway.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest video game launch in years left millions of players with a practical problem: how to eat without putting down the controller.
  • According to recent reports, rockstar Games, a unit of Take-Two Interactive, said the game brought in an estimated $3.79 billion in retail sales worldwide on its first day, which it called the biggest entertainment launch in history.
  • In a recent development, it seems like the delivery apps already planned for it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest video game launch in years left millions of players with a practical problem: how to eat without putting down the controller.

According to recent reports, rockstar Games, a unit of Take-Two Interactive, said the game brought in an estimated $3.79 billion in retail sales worldwide on its first day, which it called the biggest entertainment launch in history. With that demand, there are surely some tired people holding onto those controllers but hungry for a snack.

In a recent development, it seems like the delivery apps already planned for it. Uber Eats picked several of its Grand Theft Auto VI launch-day deals for food that could be eaten with one hand. In the U.S., the list included buy-one-get-one McNuggets at McDonald’s, boneless wings at Wingstop, pizza at Papa John’s and Whopper Jr. burgers at Burger King.

“We even picked some of our food deals with one-handed eating in mind, so fans can keep their focus on the game,” Uber President and COO Andrew Macdonald said in a statement to Fortune.

Gamers ordered accordingly. Between midnight and 5 a.m. on launch night, Uber Eats orders in Miami, the real city behind the game’s Vice City, rose more than 30% from the prior two Thursdays, Macdonald said on X. Nationwide, orders of Red Bull Watermelon rose 95%, Totino’s Pizza Rolls 54% and Ghost Sour Strips 46%. Uber told Fortune it had no separate data on one-handed food orders.

It has been revealed that doorDash reported a similar pattern. Between 9 p.m. and 2 a.m. ET, orders for chips, burgers, fries and pizza each rose more than 10% compared with the average of the six prior Wednesdays, the tech giant told Fortune. Energy drinks rose more than 20%. Miami led all major markets, with late-night orders up nearly 25%, and Philadelphia, Detroit and Atlanta also saw double-digit increases, according to DoorDash’s data dashboard. DoorDash stated it could not compare the food increases with its overall order growth.

Some of the biggest jumps were for gear, not food. Orders for controllers and gaming accessories rose 450% on DoorDash, HDMI cables 440% and headsets 70%. Searches for GTA VI on the app rose more than 940% in the week before launch.

Industry observers note that “GTA 6 is more than a game launch. It’s a cultural moment that fans have been waiting years for,” Gina Igwe, DoorDash’s vice president of brand, creative and consumer marketing, stated in a statement to Fortune.

Recent findings suggest that players who weren’t playing were watching. In its first two days, GTA VI drew more livestream watch time than any game has in its entire launch week, more than Elden Ring, Hogwarts Legacy and Cyberpunk 2077 drew in their first weeks combined, according to Streams Charts.

In a recent development, total Twitch watch time rose 61% compared with the two days before launch, the firm stated, while World of Warcraft and Counter-Strike lost about 31% of their Twitch watch time and Fortnite fell 60% on YouTube. Kick’s “Just Sleeping” category rose 176% as streamers ran round-the-clock GTA VI marathons.

Restaurant chains also moved to get a share. Popeyes is selling a Spice City sandwich, named after the game’s setting, through Nov. 22 and told players to order it through its app “between missions.” McDonald’s began taking delivery orders on Discord, the chat app many gamers use while they play. DoorDash ran offers with Wendy’s and the Cheesecake Factory, and Grubhub offered $10 off to its first 1,000 customers.

Sources indicate that analytics firm Sensor Tower expects the game to drive more than 50 million additional visits to U.S. food delivery and restaurant apps in its first 30 days, Reuters reported.

It has been revealed that neither company put a dollar figure on launch night. A rough Fortune estimate suggests the extra takeout spending was small next to the game itself. Uber and DoorDash together handled about $680 million in delivery orders a day worldwide in the third quarter, based on their earnings reports. If late-night hours make up roughly a tenth of that, and launch night lifted those orders 10% to 25%, the extra spending comes to roughly $7 million to $17 million. That’s about 1% to 2.5% of a normal day’s delivery business for the two companies, and less than half a percent of the $3.79 billion Rockstar notes the game brought in on day one.

That shift fits what economists say about events like this one. Much of the money moves from one kind of spending to another rather than appearing from nowhere. “People just rearrange how they’re spending their free time,” Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross, told Fortune before the launch.

Restaurants also had fewer hands. Missed restaurant shifts rose 92% week over week on Nov. 19, according to data from scheduling platform Harri shared with Fortune, covering 280,000 shifts. One in 14 shifts went unworked, compared with one in 27 the Thursday before, while sales at those restaurants fell less than 2%.

Grand Theft Auto VI came out Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, more than 13 years after its predecessor. Before the launch, a widely shared estimate claimed workers skipping their jobs to play would cost the U.S. economy $1 billion, a figure Matheson told Fortune he doesn’t believe. Office attendance barely moved. Wi-Fi logins at the more than 250 U.S. locations of Industrious, a coworking manufacturer owned by CBRE, fell about 5% on launch day compared with the previous three Thursdays, the company told Fortune.

Cardano-based stablecoin DJED has announced its sunset, as DJED and SHEN services will wind down on December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC.

DJED represents a crypto-backed, overcollateralized stablecoin protocol on Cardano whose US-dollar peg is maintained algorithmically against an ADA reserve (with SHEN as the reserve coin), rather than by fiat reserves.

"DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026, at 11:59 pm UTC," a DJED-focused X account wrote.

It has been revealed that ATTN: DJED & SHEN Holders DJED and SHEN services will wind down at the end of December 31, 2026 at 11:59pm UTC. Please redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN you hold before then. All redemptions are subject to the reserve ratio.

According to recent reports, customers are urged to redeem and convert any DJED and SHEN they hold before this deadline. Users are to redeem on the protocol and convert their DJED and SHEN back to ADA on the official Djed page. Users who hold DJED or SHEN in liquidity pools, lending markets, or other DeFi platforms are urged to withdraw those positions first, then redeem or swap.

The Djed team remarked all systems are fully operational and redemptions are now open, subject to the reserve ratio. It further added that the Djed protocol will be maintained and remain available until December 31, 2026. After this date, all remaining funds will be allocated to the outstanding DJED/SHEN holders once the wind-down is complete.

Sources indicate that djed’s shutdown comes almost three years after its launch, which came in 2023. The stablecoin was officially launched on the Cardano mainnet on January 31, 2023, and was developed by COTI in collaboration with the Cardano ecosystem to be used on DeFi protocols on Cardano as a stable alternative to volatile cryptocurrencies.

In positive news for the Cardano ecosystem, Monument Bank Limited has rolled out tokenized deposits on the Midnight network, marking a milestone for the network and the decentralized finance ecosystem.

At present, Monument is the first UK bank to tokenize retail deposits on a public blockchain, offering clients a 5.2% AER fixed-term return on savings directly through its existing banking app, delivering institutional onchain finance through a familiar and user-friendly banking experience.

Up to £250 million of client deposits will be represented on Midnight in this opening phase, with deposits recorded one-to-one in sterling.

A Monero token crashed 99% on Friday after 5.2 million XMR1 tokens moved from a wallet tied to its creator, triggering a massive sell-off on Hyperliquid. The token, issued through crypto swap service Wagyu, plunged from around $494 to below $1 in 35 minutes. The wallet receiving the tokens sold enough to generate $13.22 million in USDC before converting the proceeds into 7,467 ETH.

Wagyu’s wallet security and the backing behind its wrapped Monero product are being questioned. And the sell-off also sent shockwaves through the Monero market, although native XMR remained a separate asset from the collapsing XMR1 market.

🚨HYPERLIQUID WRAPPED MONERO APPEARS TO BE GETTING HACKED!@lookonchain flagged an attacker wallet that received 5.2 million $XMR1, dumped it on Hyperliquid, then used the proceeds to buy ethereum:native.So far the address has spent $13.22M USDC for 7,467 ethereum:native.… pic.twitter.com/boP1oXXmjl.

The incident began this morning when the account responsible for deploying XMR1 transferred tokens to a newly created wallet. Blockchain intelligence firm Bitquery identified three separate transfers between 04:46 and 05:16 UTC. Two transactions moved 100,000 XMR1 each, followed by a much larger transfer of 5 million tokens.

The receiving wallet had been created that morning. It began selling shortly after receiving the tokens, overwhelming buyers on Hyperliquid’s order book. XMR1 had traded near $500 throughout the previous week. Its price then collapsed to $1 within 30 minutes, leaving holders with almost nothing.

Industry observers note that bitquery traced 363,804 tokens sold for $13.5 million. The remaining 4.83 million tokens stayed in the receiving wallet during its investigation. The sell-off also exposed how concentrated XMR1’s supply had been. Before the transfers, its deployer account still controlled 93% of the token’s supply.

Hyperliquid transfers require signatures from the account’s own key, rather than an ordinary trading API wallet. This means whoever authorized the transfers likely had access to the deployer’s main key. Whether someone stole that access or used it legitimately remains unknown.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

In a recent development, the damage extended beyond traders watching XMR1 collapse on their screens. It matched the seller’s transactions against 388 accounts that purchased the dumped tokens. One buyer alone paid $3.56 million, while 27 large buyers accounted for 77% of the total proceeds.

The wallet did not leave the money sitting in USDC. It began moving funds through Hyperliquid’s bridge into Arbitrum shortly after selling.

XMR1 hack: 388 Hyperliquid buyers paid $13.50 million for a token that fell 99.8%https://t.co/k5ggHcH6Al.

According to recent reports, on Arbitrum, the wallet exchanged $13.22 million in USDC for 7,467 ETH through CoW Protocol. It then routed much of the Ethereum through Socket, Mayan, and Stargate. 6,810 ETH then arrived on Ethereum after those bridge transactions. Approximately 4,836 ETH landed in a newly created wallet that had not sent any funds onward.

According to recent reports, the investigation also identified 7,348 ETH across three wallets during its tracking window. That left a substantial amount of the proceeds sitting outside the original trading account.

It has been revealed that the incident has put Wagyu’s bridge infrastructure under scrutiny. XMR1 itself is Monero on Hyperliquid, but through Wagyu’s bridging service. Consumers can move native XMR into the service and receive XMR1 for trading. They can also reverse the process to recover their Monero.

Native XMR did not suffer the same collapse. Monero continued trading around $470–$482, while XMR1 lost virtually all its market value.

Holders now face a difficult question: Can they still exchange their remaining XMR1 for native Monero?

The incident also comes weeks after Wagyu disclosed a separate data leak on October 28. Researchers identified exposed records potentially linking crypto deposits, Monero receiving addresses, and customer IP addresses.

It has been revealed that wagyu previously remarked customer funds remained unaffected by that incident. No established connection links the October leak to Friday’s wallet transfers.

The latest investigation also uncovered another potential concern. The same deployer account controls 99.97% of ZEC1, a separate token representing Zcash on Hyperliquid.

#64710. Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Indicates Us Why

Public Markets Are Frequently Wrong. The SaaSpocalypse Indicates Us Why

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant.
  • We have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model.
  • Recent findings suggest that the SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that panics and pile-ons are a familiar pattern in the public markets, with a herd mentality wiping value from companies in an instant. Trading can swiftly become a barometer of emotions, rather than a well-informed gauge of value.

We have seen this play out with AI’s impact on software companies and the supposed end of the Software as a Service business model. The doom-laden talk of the SaaSpocalypse was noise, with little signal, and most traders were initially unable to distinguish between a company that will thrive in the AI age and one that will be decimated by it.

Recent findings suggest that the SaaSpocalypse didn’t reveal the end of software. It revealed the limits of public markets in judging its value.

This pattern erodes trust in the public markets. For companies, being publicly owned may no longer be appealing, and founders considering an exit may not view an initial public offering as the ultimate goal.

The markets have struggled to keep up with the tech advances of the AI era and judge their impact on incumbent companies. Sometimes they underreacted and ignored these developments, and other times they overreacted and panicked.

Recent findings suggest that when OpenAI launched ChatGPT to the public in November 2022, Alphabet stock was punished even though later Google emerged as a clear winner with generative AI. And with SaaS, the markets were slow to respond to the advent of generative and agentic AI through to the end of 2025.

In a recent development, the market capitalization of enterprise software companies continued to rise through this period, until January 2026 when all hell broke loose. The launch of Claude Cowork triggered a panic, especially when additional plug-ins were announced later that month that targeted specific workflows for enterprise support functions such as HR and legal.

Recent findings suggest that from there, valuations went into a tailspin, with traders treating software companies indiscriminately. Over two days, an estimated $285 billion of market capitalization was wiped from software, data analytics and financial tech companies, and by April the benchmark cloud software index — the BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud Index —  had dropped by 31% since the start of the year.

As an investor in software over many decades, I have seen this pattern many times before. AI does not mean the end of software companies. Rather, AI has driven a shift in how software is built, where user growth will come from — primarily agents rather than humans — and in the sources of defensible competitive advantage. This was always going to benefit some companies, like those deeply embedded into their customers’ core business processes, and harm others.

There were predictions of the death of SaaS, but this is the hype cycle pattern that always plays out when new technology emerges: a surge of excitement, then a correction, then productivity. In the short term, the markets overestimated the harm AI would inflict on the software sector as a whole.

According to recent reports, that is now being corrected as the markets start to realize which companies benefit from AI and which are threatened by it. At the end of October, the cloud software index was up by 26% since the start of the year and by a massive 83% since its nadir in April.

At my firm, Oxx, we never believed in the SaaSpocalypse, and the markets have recovered from this turmoil. The recovery is bifurcated with some sub sectors, like cybersecurity and data and analytics, faring well while others, like workflow management, have fallen back.

In cybersecurity, a great example is CrowdStrike, whose share price dropped by 27% in early 2026 but was up 114% between the start of the year and the end of October.

Sources indicate that the knee-jerk reactions to the latest developments with AI, however, are not just temporary market sentiment. They are part of a broader shift that has occurred since the late 1990s and accelerated in 2002 when the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was introduced to improve investor protections in the wake of the dot com crash.

It produced the unintended consequence of driving tech giant ownership from public to private markets. While the number of public companies in the U.S. has halved, private markets have grown dramatically in recent years. This is where much of the smart money can be found, along with a more accurate, and patient, assessment of software companies’ value.

In a recent development, the panic over the SaaSpocalypse has shown that the public markets aren’t an accurate reflection of the intrinsic value of many software companies. This disconnect may be causing a systematic mispricing of private company transactions — multiple transactions which had been in process early this year fell away in the wake of the false signals which came from public markets. This needs to be addressed. At the moment, few people recognize there’s a problem with the pricing function of public markets, and the first step to solving this concern is to recognize there is actually a problem.

Richard Anton is the co-founder and general partner of Oxx, a specialist software investor backing European founders on a mission to transform their industries with AI at the moment they’re readying to scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin (BTC) is facing renewed selling pressure as large holders continue to reduce their exposure, with on-chain data showing that whales have redistributed about $3.4 billion worth of the cryptocurrency over the past two weeks.

According to recent reports, notably, the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has fallen nearly 13% over the past week. The decline extends its November losses, bringing its price to a three-month low.

According to analyst Ali Martinez, large entities have sold or redistributed 48,618 BTC, valued at approximately $3.4 billion, over the past two weeks.

“Whales are still reducing their exposure. The selling hasn’t stopped yet,” Martinez tweeted.

The continued distribution suggests that major holders are yet to regain confidence in Bitcoin’s near-term prospects. With thousands of coins changing hands, the market faces the challenge of absorbing this supply without triggering further downward pressure.

Beyond whale activity, Bitcoin’s weekly performance is adding to concerns about the market’s strength.

It has been revealed that analyst Ted Pillows noted that the cryptocurrency has closed six consecutive weeks in the red, a pattern previously seen during bear markets. Trading below both moving averages further weakens its recovery prospects.

According to recent reports, “Along with that, Bitcoin failed to hold both the 200W EMA and 200W MA, which is a major sign of weakness. As long as BTC stays below these levels, sellers are in full control,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, several notable price levels have given way, leaving Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline.

Mookie, an advocate at Bitget Wallet and ambassador at Dinari Global, highlighted the cryptocurrency’s failure to maintain successive support levels, warning that $57,700 could come into focus if buyers fail to regain control.

Recent findings suggest that “If BTC can’t get back above $66.5K. we could see another drop toward the July low at $57.7K. But if buyers push it back above $66.5K we might finally see a bounce. Still not convinced we’re done dropping,” he noted.

According to recent reports, his comments put $66,500 at the center of Bitcoin’s immediate price outlook. Reclaiming that level could help buyers regain some momentum, while another rejection would leave the July low of $57,700 as a potential downside target.

Despite the prevailing bearish sentiment, some market observers believe Bitcoin could be approaching a turning point.

Gordon, founder of Crypto Crib and co-founder of Alphametrics, pointed to a potential inverse head-and-shoulders formation, suggesting that extreme pessimism could set the stage for a reversal.

“All longs have been wiped out, sentiment is max bearish, and retail is going heavy short. This is where reversal happens,” he commented.

According to recent reports, an inverse head-and-shoulders pattern is a technical formation often associated with a potential bullish reversal after an extended decline. It typically consists of three troughs, with the middle one forming the lowest point.

It has been revealed that gordon’s assessment offers a contrasting view to the warnings from other analysts. He believes that widespread bearish positioning and the liquidation of leveraged long positions could create conditions for buyers to return.

According to recent reports, however, the formation does not guarantee an immediate recovery. Bitcoin still needs enough buying interest to reverse its recent losses and reclaim key price levels.

At press time, BTC was trading at $59,299, down 5.40% over the past 24 hours.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that dario and Daniela Amodei, as well as the other cofounders—Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah—have all pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropic causes.
  • The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s seven cofounders are each worth about $20 billion on paper after the organization’s record-breaking IPO on Thursday, which also made thousands of its employees and some Silicon Valley investors extremely rich.

It has been revealed that dario and Daniela Amodei, as well as the other cofounders—Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah—have all pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropic causes. These commitments, though, are voluntary and not legally binding, according to Anthropic’s IPO filing.

The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer. On Friday, Anthropic announced that underwriters had purchased millions more shares, bringing the offering’s total to about $93.5 billion.

After pricing its shares at $83 apiece on Wednesday, the tech giant opened trading significantly higher and closed out the day at around $97. Despite shares falling to $85 on Friday afternoon amid a broader tech-fueled stock retreat, the company is still worth around $1.1 trillion—surpassing the market cap of Walmart.

In a recent development, the record IPO is great news for the cofounders and insiders who have been supporting Anthropic since it was founded in 2021. The biggest gains, though, belong to Amazon and Google, whose stakes are worth about $316 billion combined—more than twice the roughly $142 billion held by the seven cofounders. Here are some of the people and companies who stand to benefit the most.

Sources indicate that anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic’s president and chair of the board, Daniela Amodei, are among the figures most commonly associated with the company. But there are another five cofounders who are cashing in as well.

Each of its seven cofounders owns between 237 million and 241 million shares after the offering. At the stock’s price of about $85 on Friday, that means each founder has holdings worth approximately $20 billion, putting them (at least on paper) in the same league as Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who has a net worth of $21 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Each founder also sold approximately 3.38 million shares in the IPO, worth about $280 million at the offering price.

Despite owning a minority of the company’s equity, Anthropic’s cofounders control 50.1% of its shareholder voting power. The nearly equal distribution of shares among the seven founders is unusual for a Silicon Valley startup, Fortune reported.

Besides its cofounders, some Silicon Valley investors are also set to win major. Lightspeed Venture Partners, an early backer of Snapchat, led a $3.5 billion funding round in Anthropic in March 2025 when the manufacturer was valued at $61.5 billion. The VC firm owns less than 2% of the company, according to Bloomberg, yet its stake is still reportedly worth tens of billions of dollars.

Other VCs like Menlo Ventures also own a stake representing less than 2% of the firm, Bloomberg reported. Iconiq has invested more than $6 billion in Anthropic since 2025, and its stake is worth more than $26 billion, the outlet reported. Anthropic in total has more than 400 venture investors, according to PitchBook, yet no VC firm owns more than 5%, Fortune reported.

The company’s historic IPO means even some smaller stakes are now worth billions. Sound Ventures, the venture firm cofounded by Ashton Kutcher, invested about $435 million in Anthropic and owns about 0.5% of the company, Bloomberg reported. It’s unclear, though, how much Kutcher himself benefited from the trade as the actor best known for his role on That ’70s Show stepped down as general partner at the firm earlier this year.

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt also owns about 1% of Anthropic, according to Bloomberg, putting his stake’s value at about $11 billion at Friday’s share price.

According to recent reports, one early investor who won’t be reaping the rewards is FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who is serving a sentence of 25 years in prison after being convicted on fraud and conspiracy charges. Bankman-Fried has appealed his sentence to the Supreme Court. The trading firm he founded, Alameda Research, invested $500 million in Anthropic, but FTX’s bankruptcy estate sold most of its stake in 2024 to repay creditors. Among the buyers was Bankman-Fried’s former employer Jane Street, which stands to reap a multibillion-dollar windfall.

Many of the manufacturer’s roughly 5,300 employees are also getting rich thanks to generous stock-based compensation. Private-markets research firm Sacra estimated that 2,800 current and former employees could hold at least $1 million in pretax vested equity in the company at a $1.35 trillion valuation, Reuters reported.

Some of the earliest employees stand to benefit disproportionately. At least 400 early hires could hold equity worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC.

To be sure, it’s hard to estimate which employees hold how much stock because Anthropic’s IPO filing discloses aggregate equity awards but not their distribution among individual employees.

Now that Anthropic is public, non-founder employees are allowed to sell up to 10% of certain holdings, and up to another 35% following the release of Anthropic’s 2026 financial results.

Some of the biggest gains from the company’s IPO will go to two Major Tech giants, Amazon and Google. Anthropic’s IPO filing estimated that Amazon would own 14.6% of the company’s outstanding shares and Google would own 13.4%.

Sources indicate that amazon’s stake stems from billions of dollars in investments the firm has made in Anthropic dating back to 2023, around the time it had just 160 employees. At the time, Amazon committed an initial $1.25 billion as part of a deal to ultimately invest $4 billion in Anthropic. In exchange Anthropic agreed to make Amazon Web Services its primary cloud provider for critical workloads and make Claude available to AWS customers.

In total, Amazon invested $8 billion in convertible notes between 2023 and 2025 and put in another $10 billion in preferred stock in 2026.

Google has also poured billions into Anthropic, including $10 billion it invested in a financing round earlier this year and another $10 billion in a private placement alongside the IPO.

At the company’s roughly $85 per share stock price Friday, Amazon’s 1.94 billion shares would be worth about $165 billion, while Google’s 1.77 billion shares would be worth around $151 billion.

Considering the history of the transferred funds, the move has sparked speculation that the hacker might already be preparing to spend the stolen funds, further sabotaging Binance’s chances of full recovery.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

It has been revealed that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA noted.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA stated early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

Industry observers note that the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp noted Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the tech giant looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn introduces reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA stated.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • Recent findings suggest that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • According to recent reports, loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path highlights how far the probing went.

Recent findings suggest that one token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

According to recent reports, loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, indicates user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

Sources indicate that the loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction demonstrates a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

Recent findings suggest that an independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

Recent findings suggest that the numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

In a recent development, the harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Industry observers note that loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale indicates its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

According to recent reports, so the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

It has been revealed that loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

The two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

In a recent development, the loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

In a recent development, vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

Sources indicate that this looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem highlights pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

Comparing Franchises? Make Sure AI is Working For You, Not Against You

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • It has been revealed that as I’m sure you’re aware, AI is the dominant topic of discussion across the business world right now.
  • Industry observers note that in the small business world, AI has already become instrumental in supporting under-resourced entrepreneurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It has been revealed that as I’m sure you’re aware, AI is the dominant topic of discussion across the business world right now. If you haven’t already become aware of how AI is impacting your business, then you may be living under a rock.

Industry observers note that in the small business world, AI has already become instrumental in supporting under-resourced entrepreneurs. As a franchise consultant, I see this every day. Office support tools? Check. Rendering of services during a sales call? Check. Customer follow-up? Check. AI has got you covered.

Similarly, I am seeing more and more prospective franchise buyers using AI in the research phase. It’s become the first stop on the due diligence research journey, understandably so, since these AI tools are highly effective at comparing large volumes of information. However, as a franchise consultant, I’ve also seen where AI is being misused and ultimately causing more indecision and uncertainty than confidently signed franchise agreements.

According to recent reports, what I’ve discovered? AI is most useful in the middle phase of your research. Let me explain.

The due diligence process can be loosely broken down into three sections: discovery, brand comparison, and final decisions. That middle, time-intensive comparison section? These are the objective criteria you need to compare across various brands. This is where AI is your best friend. However, those two bookending pieces (discovery and the final decision)? These demand nuance and rely on intangibles that only you can decide. This is where AI is a terrible tool.

So let’s break down these three phases of franchise research and parse out where AI is beneficial and where you need to rely more on your judgment.

Right now, if you go out to three different AI platforms and ask them what franchise you should buy, you’ll get three very different answers.

According to recent reports, why? AI is terrible at franchise identification. Since AI is pulling from the internet, much of the information is promotional. The real information is hidden behind disclosure laws / walls. Furthermore, AI cannot know the actual people behind the brand or concept — it can’t meet them in person or understand the differentiators and support that only come from getting to know a brand’s team.

Industry observers note that most importantly, identifying the brands that you want to explore further requires preliminary work — work that is difficult to shortcut with AI because it’s unique to you. This is where you’ll want to first hone in on your individual requirements and goals.

What role do you want to have in the business? Do you want to work solo or hire employees? Do you want a location-based brick-and-mortar business or a service brand that provides services at varying job sites? What industries are you open to and which ones give you the ick? Answering questions like these (and many more) will help to narrow down your parameters.

Be careful not to put the cart before the horse. Take time to answer these questions before you dive into nuances of different brands. Pro tip? Consider reaching out to a franchise consultant. Working with a professional can be very useful in this phase because they will be able to help you establish and develop your criteria and apply it to a variety of viable brands.

Once you’ve identified a handful of brands you are interested in exploring further based on the criteria you determined in the initial research phase, it’s time to start a deep dive into brand comparisons. In the past, I’ve seen so many candidates toil over these comparisons, entering data into spreadsheets and trying to make sure they’re comparing apples to apples.

This is where AI is a game changer.

Historically, one of the most time-consuming and tedious parts of the due diligence process has been comparing Franchise Disclosure Documents (FDDs). This is a 23-section monster document that provides you with a full breakdown and scope of a potential franchise. This includes everything from financial projections to territory information to complicated legalities.

In a recent development, often, franchise candidates will seriously compare anywhere from 3-6 brands – that’s a lot of content to review in the FDDs. However, with AI, you can upload the brand FDDs and ask it to create a comparison of how they are similar and how they differ. Since every FDD has the same 23-section structure, it’s a good data set for AI tools to analyze and present to you in easily understandable reports, although there is no exact uniform way franchises are required to disclose information, so getting apples-to-apples comparisons requires very careful review of AI output.

Any other great uses for AI at this stage? Have it create a sensitivity analysis (best case, worst case and expected case) spreadsheet for you. Have it provide common financing options. Have it create projection models. Essentially, use it to synthesize all the information that will help you to make the final decision. Let it do the heavy labor, while you review and analyze the outputs.

At the end of the day, AI can’t make value judgments for you — that’s still more art than science. And more than anything, starting a business requires an emotional commitment and mindset shift–that is nothing AI can help you with.

Recent findings suggest that have you got that sensitivity analysis spreadsheet? That’s a fantastic tool, but a spreadsheet can’t make assumptions for you. To do this, you need to speak with individual franchisees and confirm the information during the validation stage.

Industry observers note that you had AI break down common financing options? Great, but it doesn’t understand your risk tolerance and emotional makeup. You will need to determine whether you have the financial backing and spousal support to make an investment. Additionally, AI may be able to provide a list of financial professionals in your location, but it can’t make a recommendation for that person based on actual experience — you’ll need to network or rely on your franchise consultant for that.

Ultimately, AI is a powerful tool you should absolutely use in the franchise research process. However, it’s not a catch-all replacement for either finding the right business model or the final decision-making.

In a recent development, as I’m sure you’re aware, AI is the dominant topic of discussion across the business world right now. If you haven’t already become aware of how AI is impacting your business, then you may be living under a rock.

In the small business world, AI has already become instrumental in supporting under-resourced entrepreneurs. As a franchise consultant, I see this every day. Office support tools? Check. Rendering of services during a sales call? Check. Customer follow-up? Check. AI has got you covered.

Similarly, I am seeing more and more prospective franchise buyers using AI in the research phase. It’s become the first stop on the due diligence research journey, understandably so, since these AI tools are highly effective at comparing large volumes of information. However, as a franchise consultant, I’ve also seen where AI is being misused and ultimately causing more indecision and uncertainty than confidently signed franchise agreements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

According to recent reports, langChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

Industry observers note that with its open source roots, the startup claims its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock customers into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, I didn’t build that audience to create another sales funnel. I wanted a place to share ideas, recognize the accomplishments of people across our franchise network and connect with professionals who face many of the same challenges I do. What I’ve come to appreciate is that those relationships can create opportunities long before anyone has a reason to discuss doing business together.

According to recent reports, leading my business, Anago Cleaning Systems, a franchise network of over 1,800 small business owners, has reinforced that lesson. Growth requires more than finding the next client or prospective franchise owner. It requires building a reputation that gives people a reason to trust you before the first business conversation.

Recent findings suggest that that thinking has shaped how I approach LinkedIn. My professional network has grown to more than 10,000 connections, but I don’t consider the number itself the achievement. The real value comes from the conversations, introductions and relationships that develop when people know what you stand for.

Here are four lessons I’ve learned about making professional relationships part of a long-term growth strategy.

Too many entrepreneurs treat professional networking as another sales channel. Their content focuses on what they’re selling, why it’s better and how someone can purchase it.

Industry observers note that yet people generally don’t join professional communities hoping to receive more sales pitches. They’re looking for valuable information, new perspectives and connections that help them navigate their own challenges.

Industry observers note that my monthly newsletter explores scaling businesses, executive leadership, organizational culture and franchising. Rather than making every edition about franchise opportunities, I focus on sharing lessons that business owners can apply regardless of their industry.

According to recent reports, that approach gives people a reason to stay connected. Someone may never become a client or franchise owner, but a useful idea can lead to a conversation, an introduction or an opportunity neither person anticipated.

Sources indicate that some of the most meaningful stories we share through LinkedIn aren’t about corporate leadership. They’re about the independent franchise owners building businesses within our network.

Recognizing their milestones, highlighting their accomplishments and sharing moments from our seminars and events provides a perspective that corporate messaging alone cannot deliver.

In a recent development, prospective business owners want to understand the people behind an organization. They want to see how individuals are growing, what support looks like and whether the culture aligns with their expectations.

In a recent development, for entrepreneurs, there’s a broader lesson here. Your customers, employees and business partners often provide the most compelling evidence of your organization’s value. Giving them visibility creates a more credible picture of the business than repeatedly telling people how successful you are.

One thing I’ve noticed through building my LinkedIn network is how difficult it can be to predict where a professional relationship will lead. Someone might initially connect with me because of an article about leadership, begin following my newsletter and eventually develop an interest in our franchise network. Another connection might work in commercial property management and find value in the facility management trends we share.

Sources indicate that that’s why I’ve never viewed LinkedIn as simply a sales tool. I use it to maintain relationships with people who have different interests, professional backgrounds and business goals. Those connections create opportunities for conversations that might not otherwise happen.

Recent findings suggest that as our network has grown, I’ve also come to appreciate how closely sales, marketing and recruiting overlap. A prospective franchise owner, commercial client, or future employee may first encounter our organization through the same piece of content. What happens next depends on the relationship we build.

I recently explored LinkedIn Premium All-in-One with that in mind. Based on the criteria I set, it suggested professionals whose backgrounds aligned with leadership, entrepreneurship and franchise development. I reviewed their experience and looked for shared interests that could make a future conversation worthwhile. Rather than approaching those connections with an agenda, I wanted to understand where a professional relationship might naturally begin.

The exercise reinforced why bringing sales, marketing and hiring capabilities together makes sense for entrepreneurs. A connection that begins around a shared business interest may eventually lead to a customer relationship, a partnership or a conversation about joining the organization. Tools that support those overlapping responsibilities can make it easier to spot opportunities without treating every interaction as a transaction.

It has been revealed that publishing content is only part of the equation. The conversations it creates can be just as valuable.

Sharing articles, discussing leadership challenges and highlighting developments across our franchise network help me stay connected with people whose experiences differ from my own.

That exchange matters. Entrepreneurs can become so focused on explaining their businesses that they overlook the opportunity to listen. A thoughtful comment, an unexpected question or a different perspective can reveal something worth exploring further.

Consistency is more vital than volume. You don’t need to post constantly or turn every professional interaction into content. You need to contribute often enough, and with enough substance, that people understand what you stand for.

Leading a large franchise organization has taught me that growth rarely comes from a single strategy. It requires strong operations, capable people, effective marketing and relationships built on trust.

Professional networking is one part of that larger picture, but it’s an increasingly valuable one. Platforms such as LinkedIn give entrepreneurs opportunities to establish credibility and maintain relationships beyond their immediate markets. The challenge is resisting the temptation to measure success only through connections, impressions or immediate leads.

The relationships that eventually create meaningful opportunities often begin with something much simpler: an idea worth sharing, a conversation worth continuing or an accomplishment worth recognizing.

It has been revealed that if you’re thinking about how to build those relationships more intentionally, LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to grow your network, build credibility and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to see what fits the way you work.

When people already understand your perspective and trust what you bring to the conversation, the next business opportunity doesn’t have to begin with an introduction. It can begin with an existing relationship.

What I’ve come to appreciate is that those relationships can create opportunities long before anyone has a reason to discuss doing business together.

Leading my business, Anago Cleaning Systems, a franchise network of over 1,800 small business owners, has reinforced that lesson. Growth requires more than finding the next client or prospective franchise owner. It requires building a reputation that gives people a reason to trust you before the first business conversation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

According to recent reports, she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Recent findings suggest that paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers remarked they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates stated Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

According to recent reports, she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In a recent development, in its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook.
  • Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

In a recent development, over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

In a recent development, most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

“She’s much more conservative,” one investor remarked of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”.

It has been revealed that nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, founder of the hardware company Ghost, mentioned.

It has been revealed that for instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya remarked of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”.

According to recent reports, it’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the tech giant does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two upcoming chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.).

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

According to recent reports, dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he stated. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

In a recent development, under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC noted. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the fresh companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval mentioned. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”.
