In a recent development, MEXC notes user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange claims it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

It has been revealed that two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

Industry observers note that the other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN notes the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

Recent findings suggest that the charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN states MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

Industry observers note that the order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary consumers anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Recent findings suggest that section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

Sources indicate that one provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

Industry observers note that for most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN states plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

It has been revealed that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Sources indicate that predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

According to recent reports, finCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

In a recent development, three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

According to recent reports, the largest Shiba Inu traders and investors moved more than 6 billion SHIB to exchange addresses out of the blue, potentially chasing liquidity instead of holding. For now, SHIB hasn't reacted to the transfer, as moving SHIB to exchanges doesn't guarantee immediate selling.

It could be a sign, though: according to historical data, whale activity quite often corresponds to market improvements for SHIB. Those whales might have certain data that we don't.

Sources indicate that whenever the price moves up, whales who accumulated previously liquidate their holdings and successfully move on. However, it's not a paramount rule that can't be broken. We might always see a flip in that tendency.

6 billion SHIB is not an unseen number, and investors quite often simply redistribute their holdings, so it's not something you should worry about.

Recent findings suggest that from a holder perspective, acting immediately on transfers like this is most likely not the go-to decision right now. The current composition of the market is far from bullish, but a mere 6 billion transfer isn't going to change the course of SHIB right here and right now.

Retail investors aren't moving on par with those 6 billion, data suggests, as inflow and outflow data show neutrality rather than leaning in one direction or the other.

The timing of the transfer is somewhat interesting: the market isn't recovering, SHIB is losing the ground it has gained in the last few days, and, unfortunately, the SHIB sent to exchanges might contribute to a further price drop.

SHIB is oversold, clearly, but the presence of supply just sitting elsewhere essentially enables the possibility of a quick drop way sooner than we might think.

The key here is the lack of proper psychological and technical levels that might help the price recover or at least form a range.

A highly contagious strain of “GTA flu” is spreading through U.S. workplaces. Symptoms include sudden PTO requests, controller cramps and an urge to visit Vice City. The outbreak began yesterday, when Grand Theft Auto VI rolled out after a 13-year wait, according to Newsweek.

BambooHR, analyzing data on 3.4 million U.S. workers, saw a 13% spike in pre-approved time-off requests for November 19. Global payroll tech giant Remote reported 32% more time off booked than the same day last year, calling it the biggest non-holiday leave spike of 2026, according to USA Today. Gen Z was the hardest-hit group, booking the day at nearly twice last year’s rate.

Some employers have given up fighting it. Logitech gifted its 7,000 employees a paid gaming day, and CEO Hanneke Faber intends to play GTA VI on launch day. At Fort Stewart in Georgia, at least 43 soldiers reenlisted in exchange for a four-day pass timed to the launch.

In a recent development, economists disagree on the damage. One widely circulated estimate puts the productivity loss at $1 billion. Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross, tells Newsweek he takes “no concern” with that figure in the short run. But over time, he says, planned absences mean “zero productivity loss,” since workers are swapping one day off for another.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.
  • Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the organization’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

According to recent reports, customers cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it introduced publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of people. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

Flaming Hydra’s new Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a substantial promise: A fresh Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”.

That’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a upcoming e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor, Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”.

Bustillos told me that these problems have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself — for example, when Tal Lavin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos stated Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”.

“AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”.

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”.

Sources indicate that this is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

Industry observers note that “E-books are books,” Bustillos stated. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”.

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”.

So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Industry observers note that flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

The Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Recent findings suggest that similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos noted she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Ranganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

“We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she remarked. “Those things go hand in hand.”.

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

Industry News: I Didn’t Have a TV At Home — So I Built a Computer At Age 13 to Compensate. Now My Startup Is On Track to Unlock $1 Billion in Value.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C.
  • Industry observers note that in his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions.
  • I’ve always been someone who has had high self-agency, a huge amount of self-trust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C. Willenbrock, founder of AIVC, an AI firm that rebuilds operational and service-focused businesses with AI. Willenbrock, 35, describes himself as the “tech rebel” of his family because both of his parents and his brother had long careers in finance. He started off in finance but ended up taking a different path deeper into computer science and AI.

Industry observers note that in his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions. He served as its chief product officer until AI recruitment startup Stella.ai acquired it in 2018. Willenbrock began building AIVC, short for AI Value Creation, in October 2025 and is still working at the startup as a builder. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

I’ve always been someone who has had high self-agency, a huge amount of self-trust. I grew up in Denver and somehow found myself many years later in New York City.

At an early age, you could call me the tech rebel in the family. The rebel in me came out early. We didn’t have TVs growing up in our household, so when it came time to try and figure out how to get a TV in the bedroom, I just built a computer with TV on it. I was 13 years old.

It has been revealed that early on, I was motivated by achievement and success, and I understood those pretty conventionally. I went to Dartmouth, then Morgan Stanley, then into growth equity. Those were paths I understood and respected.

In growth equity, I was basically a glorified cold-caller, talking to founders about businesses they had built. That opened up my sense of what a career could look like. I was curious about the problems they were solving, and I wanted a more direct hand in the outcome.

Over time, that took me into building companies, product development and work that was harder to explain with one job title.

It has been revealed that the connecting thread was wanting to solve problems and have a direct hand in the outcome. It took time to stop measuring my choices against what looked like a prestigious career and start trusting what genuinely motivated me.

In a recent development, my first business was Stickworks (started in middle school), stringing lacrosse sticks for people in the neighborhood and on my brother’s teams. I hadn’t even started playing lacrosse myself; I just loved stringing the sticks. I was much less interested in collecting the money, which turned out to be a fairly notable part of running a business.

CompIQ, the compensation benchmarking and pay-equity business I started later, taught me something harder. I put all my savings into it and made a lot of mistakes early on, including hiring mistakes. Eventually, the business was on a strong trajectory, and I had brilliant people on the team.

I never intended to start AIVC. It grew out of a persistent problem that I couldn’t stop working on. Through my work with companies and private equity firms, I kept seeing the same gap. People could identify opportunities for AI, but turning those opportunities into a better business required someone to bring together technology, people, operating decisions and responsibility for the result. That work kept falling between organizations.

Industry observers note that my view is that AI is making more of the analytical and financial-engineering work in investing easier to reproduce. The hard part is understanding how much value you can create in a particular business and then actually creating it. That was the work I wanted to pursue.

In a recent development, our first clients came in 2025 through relationships I had built over years. A few private equity firms gave us access to their portfolio companies, and we also had clients outside that network. They knew me and trusted me to deliver.

Industry observers note that that history mattered. We had multiple paying clients before AIVC formally introduced in April 2026. From the beginning, I wanted our commercial approach tied to outcomes, because I had seen companies pay a lot for work without getting the result they needed. The proposition was that we would put the right people on the problem and take responsibility for making the business better.

Revenue for AIVC’s first year is in the eight figures.

In a recent development, but the number we run the company on is the value we create for clients, because we only earn when they do. We align our incentives with the client — because ultimately our goal is to create value (it’s in our name: AI Value Creation). We get paid when our clients win, so our revenue trails the value we create, sometimes by a lot.

Industry observers note that this year we will have created more than $1 billion in enterprise value across our engagements. Eighty percent of the quantified potential is tied to revenue or capacity-led growth, not cost-cutting. This is extremely notable to us because most of the AI story revolves around cost-cutting and human displacement. We want to unlock growth by unlocking human capacity — making humans more human.

Industry observers note that be honest about the support that makes taking a risk possible. I’ve taken some big risks, and I haven’t always judged them correctly.

My parents were the backbone that allowed me to take them. They invested time, effort, money and confidence in me. I knew it was okay if I failed.

They’ve worked together for almost 40 years and built their wealth management business within a larger organization. My career has looked very different, but their backing has been fundamental to it. I also have a close group of friends who have been there through the uncertainty.

Industry observers note that that’s part of what I want AIVC to provide for other people. There are brilliant people who want to build something and own a meaningful part of the outcome, but making that move can mean taking on more risk than they can carry alone. I want us to provide capital, teammates, resources and someone who will stand behind them when the first attempt doesn’t work.

In a recent development, get specific about what you’re good at and what you’re bad at. That affects who you hire, what you delegate and where you spend your own time. If you can’t name your weaknesses, it’s easy to build a team of people like you and leave the same gaps uncovered.

Sources indicate that then be someone those people can rely on. You don’t have to be the smartest person in the room. You do have to do the small things well, including the work you don’t feel like doing, and keep improving when things are going well enough that you could get comfortable.

Industry observers note that before taking a substantial risk, work through the best outcome, the most likely outcome and the worst outcome — and what you would actually do in each. Taking a risk and understanding it should go together.

It has been revealed that talent gets you noticed, and habits get you where you’re going. Do the small, boring things right every day, the ones nobody claps for, because they compound. Most founders overestimate what one big move can do and underestimate what 1,000 small ones will do.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with R.C. Willenbrock, founder of AIVC, an AI firm that rebuilds operational and service-focused businesses with AI. Willenbrock, 35, describes himself as the “tech rebel” of his family because both of his parents and his brother had long careers in finance. He started off in finance but ended up taking a different path deeper into computer science and AI.

Sources indicate that in his mid-20s, he co-founded CompIQ, a startup focused on helping employers make compensation decisions. He served as its chief product officer until AI recruitment startup Stella.ai acquired it in 2018. Willenbrock began building AIVC, short for AI Value Creation, in October 2025 and is still working at the startup as a builder. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

Sources indicate that I’ve always been someone who has had high self-agency, a huge amount of self-trust. I grew up in Denver and somehow found myself many years later in New York City.

The Single Asset Vault amendment on the XRP Ledger is getting closer to activation on the mainnet as validator support builds for the network’s preparation to enable better DeFi functionality.

In a recent development, according to data from XRPScan, the SingleAssetVault amendment, or XLS-65, has received yes votes from 25 of 35 trusted validators, right now standing at 71.43% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of 35 votes (29) to start its 14-day countdown to activation. That means it needs four more votes to get there and could reach the magic number before the end of 2026.

The XRP Ledger’s amendment process requires a proposed amendment to be approved by more than 80% of trusted validators for 14 days before it is implemented. Validator support may shift during this time, and if the required 80% threshold is lost, activation may be delayed.

Industry observers note that the Single Asset Vault amendment creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. The amendment introduces a Vault object that defines the state of a tokenized vault, and the Vault entry is one of the ledger entry types it provides.

Recent findings suggest that the Vault object holds notable information such as available assets, shares, total value, and other relevant information. Owners can create a Vault object with the VaultCreate transaction; the Vault object is tracked in an Owner Directory owned by the Vault Owner account.

The XRP Ledger lending amendment has gained additional yes votes. According to XRPScan, the LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment, also known as XLS-66, has received 24 yes votes out of 35 trusted validators, meaning it has 68.57% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of the 35 votes (29) to trigger a 14-day activation countdown.

This implies that there are five votes left for it to reach this threshold, with the possibility of it securing the required number of votes before the end of 2026 as well.

According to XRP enthusiasts, LendingProtocolV1_1 represents the biggest amendment for unlocking capital and liquidity on the XRP Ledger and is anticipated by institutional and retail users.

  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really major step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

In a recent development, zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Recent findings suggest that boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles mentioned. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “crucial step toward undersea superiority.”.

Sources indicate that “Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Next year, Zeno Power intends to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

Sources indicate that the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The firm is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

It has been revealed that since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

According to recent reports, bitcoin price has fallen below $62,000 for the first time since early July, extending a brutal November selloff as institutional investors pull billions from the market. BTC touched $61,270 just now, before recovering slightly to trade around $61,700.

Yesterday’s $582.2 million outflow from US spot Bitcoin ETFs added another blow, bringing November withdrawals close to $3.5 billion.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest single-day outflow since launching. The same session saw $727 million in crypto liquidations, with bullish traders absorbing most of the damage.

Institutional demand is weakening, leveraged buyers are being forced out, and the Federal Reserve’s increasingly hawkish outlook is making speculative assets less attractive.

Bitcoin is now approaching $60,000, a level that could determine if the correction finds a floor or develops into something uglier.

Industry observers note that the ETF withdrawals are arguably the biggest concern for Bitcoin holders right now. Spot Bitcoin ETFs became an notable source of institutional demand after launching in January 2024. Their buying helped absorb available supply and gave traditional investors a regulated route into the market.

That demand is now moving in the opposite direction. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost more than $1.1 billion this week alone. November’s cumulative withdrawals have approached $3.5 billion.

In a recent development, the pressure extends beyond ETFs. Rising Treasury yields and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase in December have encouraged investors to reduce exposure to assets that offer no regular income.

Meanwhile, derivatives traders are taking heavy losses. CoinGlass data revealed more than $700 million in liquidations across crypto markets over 24 hours. Long positions accounted for 86% of the total.

Bitcoin itself recorded nearly $202 million in liquidations, with bullish traders suffering the majority of forced closures.

This creates a difficult environment for buyers. Falling prices trigger liquidations, which create additional selling pressure and push prices lower. The reduction in open interest also suggests excessive leverage is being flushed from the market.

In a recent development, the immediate battle is around $60,000. Bitcoin needs to reclaim $62,000 and establish support above it before bulls can confidently argue that the latest breakdown was temporary.

There are three possible scenarios:.

Scenario 1: Bitcoin loses $60K and heads toward $58K or $53K.

This is the bearish outcome. A decisive break below $60,000 could trigger another wave of stop-loss orders and leveraged liquidations.

The next downside area sits around $58,000, while more aggressive technical projections point toward $53,700.

Scenario 2: Bitcoin stabilizes between $60K and $62K.

This would give buyers time to absorb available supply without immediately reversing the entire November decline.

The liquidation wave has already removed considerable leverage from the market. If ETF withdrawals begin slowing, Bitcoin could establish a trading range before attempting another recovery.

A recovery above $62,000 would provide the first meaningful sign that sellers are losing control. A move toward $65,000 would then become possible, followed by resistance around $68,000.

Consistent ETF inflows, improving market sentiment, and a weaker dollar would strengthen this scenario. Without those developments, any rebound risks becoming another opportunity for sellers to exit.

For existing holders, the decision depends heavily on their entry price, investment horizon, and exposure. Long-term holders who bought substantially below current prices have more room to withstand volatility. Selling simply because Bitcoin crossed a psychological threshold risks locking in profits or losses without knowing whether the broader investment thesis has changed.

It has been revealed that however, investors holding leveraged positions face a different problem. Falling prices can trigger forced liquidations regardless of their long-term convictions. Reducing leverage and protecting available capital should take priority over waiting for a rebound.

Bitcoin price remains vulnerable to another leg down. The $60,000 level is no longer just a psychological milestone. It is where the next major battle between buyers and sellers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines.
  • So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data reveals.
  • To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

So far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data reveals. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Recent findings suggest that much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

According to recent reports, by far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old tech giant raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor says it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

According to recent reports, in this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

It has been revealed that agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, unveiled a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of massive rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Recent findings suggest that typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual manufacturer highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Industry observers note that institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

In a recent development, founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

In a recent development, companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other. Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an vital regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

As an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off. This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

Early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction. A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Industry observers note that founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Industry observers note that has the founder or company addressed these problems in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

These challenges make the earliest stages of manufacturer formation particularly crucial. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

In a recent development, at Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the company is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

According to recent reports, that means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

AI and new distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

According to recent reports, the traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

Moving quickly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

Industry observers note that for investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a tech giant needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

The most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Although XRP has achieved a sharp price rally after the severe price correction seen in the past months, its recent recovery has yet to influence the performance of its ETF market.

Latest data from SoSoValue indicates that momentum across the XRP ETF market has remained slow as the funds have continued to post massive withdrawals during each trading session in recent days.

Data indicates that the XRP ETFs managed by Canary Capital and Grayscale recorded combined withdrawals of $6.14 million during their latest trading session on November 17.

This also represents the total daily net outflows recorded on that day as only the two funds were active while the rest of the XRP ETF products remained muted with zero participation from investors.

While this means that investors have continued to withdraw their funds despite XRP attempting to reclaim the $1 price level, Canary Capital's XRP ETF saw the highest withdrawal of the day.

Notably, the fund recorded over 5 million XRP, worth about $5.01 million, in daily outflows, while Grayscale's XRP ETF followed with just $1.12 million in outflows.

Although Bitwise did not record any inflow or outflow on this day, the firm still stands as XRP’s biggest ETF manager as it controls over $392.64 million in net assets as of this date.

Despite its dominance in the XRP ETF market, Bitwise has remained muted all week, showing zero daily participation since November 9, when it posted its highest-ever daily outflow of $9.40 million.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup notes it has secured design wins with U.S.
  • India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup notes it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

According to recent reports, the Upcoming Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) mentioned in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Sources indicate that kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Industry observers note that bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor noted. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indusbridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor mentioned, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Recent findings suggest that bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup intends to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor stated. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology manufacturer out of India,” Kapoor stated.

In 2024, Bharat Semi declared aims for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

In a recent development, the project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The upcoming funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with massive financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • In a recent development, for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with massive financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

In a recent development, for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond manufacturer agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

In a recent development, the five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei noted Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he remarked.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the firm to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

Industry observers note that what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has stated it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will upgrade the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text.
  • According to recent reports, four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft.
  • The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

According to recent reports, four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

It has been revealed that the abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

It has been revealed that review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record indicates what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

According to recent reports, rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

Recent findings suggest that the SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Sources indicate that rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ states a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move rapidly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

In a recent development, the sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

In a recent development, until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Asset manager Bitwise has filed an S-1 with the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that zcash is often called a "more secret" version of Bitcoin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Asset manager Bitwise has filed an S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a spot Zcash (ZEC) exchange-traded fund. The document appeared in the SEC's database on Nov. 17, 2026. On Wednesday, ZEC rose to $975 before it pulled back to around $927.

Recent findings suggest that zcash is often called a "more secret" version of Bitcoin. According to the S-1, the Zcash network supports two types of transactions, and the "shielded" ones use a form of zero-knowledge cryptography known as zk-SNARKs. Holders of shielded Zcash "may selectively disclose transaction information to third parties," the filing indicates.

Industry observers note that bitwise's fund will not use this feature. "The Trust does not engage in shielded transactions in connection with its activities," according to the document.

It has been revealed that the shares are expected to list on the Dallas-based Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) under the ticker ZEC. According to the S-1, Coinbase Custody Trust Manufacturer will act as the Zcash custodian, and BNY Mellon will serve as the cash custodian. Bitwise also wrote that "the Trust will not stake or otherwise seek to derive additional Zcash from its holdings." The sponsor fee in the filing is listed as "0.___% per annum.".

In the risk section of the S-1, Bitwise wrote that "a number of digital asset trading platforms have delisted Zcash, restricted trading in Zcash or declined to support Zcash." According to the filing, many of these platforms cited regulatory or compliance concerns.

The platforms that still support Zcash "do so only with respect to transparent addresses and do not permit deposits or withdrawals to or from shielded addresses," the document indicates. Bitwise also pointed to latest EU rules that take effect on July 10, 2027. According to the S-1, the rules will "prohibit credit institutions, financial institutions and crypto-asset service providers in the European Union" from keeping accounts in such assets.

Sources indicate that bitwise CIO Matt Hougan named Zcash one of his top three assets for the decade in September, alongside Bitcoin and tokenization projects. Three days before the S-1 filing, he called ZEC a "golden mean" between open Bitcoin and anonymous Monero in an interview.

Recent findings suggest that grayscale's Zcash fund (ZCSH) has traded on NYSE Arca since August 2026, and the Winklevoss brothers filed for their own Zcash ETF on Nasdaq in October. ZCSH held $496.79 million as of the Nov. 17 close, according to SoSoValue. The fund has attracted $168.76 million in net inflows since its launch, and it recorded no inflows on Nov. 17, when Bitwise filed its S-1.

Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious proposal to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he stated.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Recent findings suggest that nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek remarked. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

According to recent reports, for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he remarked. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

In a recent development, after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk manufacturer developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd noted. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Sources indicate that redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In a recent development, in 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in fresh natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Sources indicate that redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who stated the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he remarked, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The organization landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Industry observers note that team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd noted there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

According to recent reports, the firm now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

Recent findings suggest that “This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.
