📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, has expressed his concerns about the storage of sensitive personal data after Japanese authorities called on rental car services to delete customers' identity documents following a massive data breach.

It has been revealed that in his latest X post, CZ pointed to a Nov. 18 notice issued by Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). The notice urges rental car services to be cautious about unnecessarily storing images of driver’s licenses and other government-issued identification documents.

The recent call by Japanese authorities comes after a massive cybersecurity attack on a popular Japanese car-sharing service called Times Car, operated by Park24 Group.

The incident began when the company noticed suspicious activity on its system on Sept. 25. As a result, it introduced an investigation into whether someone had accessed its systems without permission, potentially exposing customer data.

Recent findings suggest that as per the disclosure by Park24 on Oct. 23, about 6.63 million customer accounts were impacted by the breach.

Worse, the investigation uncovered evidence that hackers had transmitted 1,464,800 encrypted images of identification documents, including driver’s licenses, to external locations.

In a recent development, besides that, another 891,602 encrypted images of identification documents were accessed suspiciously. However, investigators found no evidence that these additional ID images had been transmitted outside the manufacturer’s systems.

Industry observers note that japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission issued its notice on Nov. 18, focusing on the risks of retaining sensitive personal data even after its original purpose has been fulfilled.

The regulatory body stressed that storing unnecessary identification images could significantly worsen the consequences of cyberattacks.

Although Japan’s latest warning specifically targets the rental car industry, CZ’s decision to share his concerns about this issue also raises questions about personal data protection in the crypto industry.

Generally, centralized crypto exchanges require users to go through a Know Your Customer (KYC) process to access their trading platforms.

Depending on the platform and jurisdiction, these processes may require users to provide photos of their passports, driver’s licenses, national ID cards, and other sensitive information.

This kind of sensitive data can be a goldmine for cybercriminals, who can exploit stolen personal information for various activities such as identity theft, phishing attacks, fraudulent registrations, and more.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that there is an old story in Stephen Hawking’s “A Brief History of Time” about a scientist lecturing on the universe when a woman in the audience insists that the world rests on the back of a giant turtle.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The financing of the AI buildout is shifting from equity to debt, and those who invested through the telecom bubble may recognize what that shift tends to mean.

Industry observers note that there is an old story in Stephen Hawking’s “A Brief History of Time” about a scientist lecturing on the universe when a woman in the audience insists that the world rests on the back of a giant turtle. Asked what the turtle stands on, she replies that it’s “turtles all the way down.” Her response is what philosophers call infinite regress — a chain of claims in which each one rests on another of the same kind and solid ground never arrives.

According to recent reports, I think of it when I look at the AI buildout because its logic has taken the same shape. Valuations support borrowing, and borrowing builds capacity. The capacity then becomes proof that the valuations were right, so each claim stands on the one beneath it.

Over the past year, more of the stack has started running on debt rather than equity, and in my experience, that crossing is the moment the telecom bubble becomes the relevant history given that debt may change how these stories end.

Until recently, the AI buildout was largely an equity-financed story, with venture investment reaching record levels.

Recent findings suggest that crunchbase data indicates global venture funding totaled $679 billion through the first three quarters of 2026, the highest amount ever recorded for that period. AI companies attracted $102 billion in the third quarter alone, accounting for roughly 64% of global venture funding. A record 27 companies raised rounds of $1 billion or more during the quarter, collectively accounting for about a third of that total.

Sources indicate that equity financing carries significant risks, but unlike debt, it generally does not impose fixed repayment obligations. When investments underperform, equity investors typically absorb losses through declining valuations, while companies may retain greater flexibility to pursue their long-term strategies.

In a recent development, that debt is now arriving in size. Meta sold $30 billion of bonds last October in one of the largest corporate debt sales on record, then returned for $25 billion more in April, with investors reportedly demanding more compensation the second time. Amazon, Alphabet and Oracle have each borrowed tens of billions of their own, and Meta’s giant Louisiana data-center campus was financed with a record $27 billion bond raised by a joint-venture partner rather than by Meta itself. Morgan Stanley expects the significant AI and cloud companies to spend about $3 trillion on infrastructure through 2028, with only about half of it expected to come from their own cash flow. The rest has to come from somewhere, and increasingly I think that somewhere is the bond market and private credit.

I watched the earlier version of this from a front-row seat, first as a venture capitalist in the late 1990s and since then as a lender to growth-stage technology companies. Telecom borrowed staggering sums against a demand forecast that was widely repeated and rarely checked, the famous claim that internet traffic was doubling every 100 days.

Traffic was actually doubling about once a year, spectacular growth but a fraction of what the borrowing assumed. By 2002 the telecom sector carried roughly $1 trillion in debt, much of which the chairman of the FCC told Congress would never be repaid, and WorldCom had entered what was then the largest bankruptcy in American history.

According to recent reports, much of the fiber the industry laid sat dark for years and was finally put to work by buyers who paid pennies on the dollar for it in bankruptcy, through a decade of restructurings and private mergers that rebuilt entire cap tables. Some companies survived that process, and many did not.

The echo that concerns me most is the demand narrative. Today’s version holds that data centers are effectively leased before they are built and that the only real mistake is building too little. That may prove correct, but it is repeated with the same uniformity the traffic forecast enjoyed in 1999, and much of it rests on projections supplied by the companies doing the building. What has changed in recent months is that investors have begun demanding an answer.

Anthropic is now public, and once companies of that scale report financial results every quarter, investors can check the demand story against audited numbers.

It has been revealed that some may argue, reasonably, that my comparison fails and that the companies doing the largest borrowing may be among the most profitable enterprises ever built, with cash flows the telecom carriers never approached. A few AI companies also appear to be reaching revenue scale faster than any businesses before them.

Industry observers note that and the internet really did change everything, just as the traffic really did arrive. All of that may be true, and none of it answers the question I think a lender has to ask, which is whether the cash arrives on the schedule the debt requires. Equity can generally wait out a wrong timeline in a way debt cannot, and when borrowed money builds capacity faster than revenue arrives to service it, in my opinion, the correction tends to come through restructurings rather than quiet markdowns.

None of this is a prediction that the AI buildout must end the way telecom did. The most durable lesson of the telecom bust, in my view, concerned capital structure, which decided who was still standing when demand finally caught up with capacity, long after the technology itself had been vindicated. I have spent years arguing that growth companies fear debt more than they should, and I still believe it, but the argument has always been conditional.

Debt serves borrowers whose obligations are sized to revenue they can see and lenders who underwrite fundamentals instead of narratives, and it treats everyone else harshly. I believe the borrowing stacked beneath the AI boom will be judged by that standard. Every assumption in the stack may well hold, but what I learned the last time is that once investors begin asking what the turtles are standing on, they rarely stop until they reach something solid.

Sources indicate that david Spreng is the founder, co-CEO and co-CIO of Runway Growth Capital. He has more than 30 years of experience as a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and growth debt lender, has been involved in the formation and development of nearly 50 technology companies, and has appeared four times on the Forbes Midas List of top venture capitalists. He co-founded Decathlon Capital Partners in 2010, served on the board of the National Venture Capital Association and has participated as a panelist at the World Economic Forum in Davos.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And it’s Friday! [Throws frisbee into tree.].

Before we dive into the newsletter, one more bit of great news about our upcoming event (which we promise we’ll stop talking about soon): Michael Grimes, the star tech banker from Morgan Stanley at the center of Uber’s IPO (and Facebook IPO, and Slack’s and Spotify’s), has been persuaded to come and talk about direct listings, which we’re very excited about. If you’re as confused as we are about whether these make sense for more than a couple of companies each year (current status: we don’t think they do), you won’t want to miss this rare conversation with “Wall Street’s Silicon Valley whisperer.”.

According to recent reports, note that seats are almost gone. Giant thanks to NextWorld, the early-stage enterprise-focused firm that’s hosting all of us; to KCPR, the boutique tech PR and strategy firm; and to Carta, a platform that helps companies and VCs manage their cap tables, valuations, investments, and equity plans, for their support.

Ben Horowitz,  the co-founder of the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, has a fresh book coming out this coming Monday titled “What You Do is Who You Are,” that takes a look at how to create “culture” at a company.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a word that’s thrown around a lot but that’s very hard to grasp, let alone implement in a sustainable way. Horowitz learned firsthand as a CEO how elusive it can be when he took stock of his company, only to discover it was made up of “screamers who intimidated their people,” others who “neglected to give any feedback,” and at least one compulsive liar who excelled at sucking up to Horowitz and also making up stories from whole cloth.

Horowitz claims creating culture was a missing part of his education, and in this latest book — a follow-up to his best-selling “The Hard Thing About Hard Things” — he does his best to fill that gap for other CEOs, using his own experience, as well as lessons gleaned from historical figures Toussaint Louverture and Genghis Khan, along with Shaka Senghor, a contemporary who served time for murder and today is a criminal justice reform advocate.

Sources indicate that it’s an instructive and novel combination, and we suggest picking up the book, especially if you love history. In the meantime, we sat down recently with Horowitz to talk about its timing and whether some of the biggest cultural blow-ups in the startup industry — Uber and WeWork — could have been avoided. These excerpts have been edited for length and clarity. Note that we’ll have more of the conversation — including Horowitz’s thoughts about dual-class shares —  for readers of Extra Crunch on Monday.

You’ve just written a book about culture that’s coming out just as a lot of questions are being raised about culture because of WeWork. What happened there?

Industry observers note that [Cofounder Adam Neumann] had a certain kind of culture there. He had some holes — some great strengths and great holes. And sometimes that happens. When you’re really good at part of it, you can delude yourself into thinking that you’ve got everything you need when you have some massive incompleteness.

Adam is so amazing. Like, the way they got all the money and everything. And the vision was so spectacular. And everybody there believed it, and they recruited some phenomenal talent. But when you’re that optimistic, it does help to have something in the culture that states [allows] people to bring you the bad news, like, if the accounting is all over the place or what have you.

In a recent development, as with Uber’s Travis Kalanick, whose culture also came under fire, Neumann operated in very plain sight. He wasn’t hiding who he was or what he was spending.

Sources indicate that right, everybody knew how Travis was running the company. Everyone in Silicon Valley knew, let alone everyone on the board. The culture was published. You can look up Uber’s values [from that period].

Recent findings suggest that travis designed, I think, a really compelling culture, and believed in it, and published it. And the consequences of what he was missing were also super well-known. It’s only when board members think people are coming after them that [they take an interest in these things].

What are the biggest lessons in these two cases?

Industry observers note that I obviously know more about Uber [as a Lyft investor who follows the space]. In Uber’s case, it’s a very subtle thing. Travis had a really good code. But he had a bug in it.

In a recent development, I think it was reported that, like, Travis encouraged bad behavior. I don’t think he did at all. I just think he didn’t make it clear that legal and ethical [considerations] were more important than competitiveness. As a result, when left to their own devices, in a distributed organization where there was a lot of distributed power, that combination had people doing things that were out of bounds.

Industry observers note that and he was making everybody so much money. And the organization was growing so fast that, for the board members, I suspect they were like, ‘As long as it’s making money, I’m not going to worry about what happens next.’.

Industry observers note that to me, the unfair part is, like, they shouldn’t get any credit at the end. Whatever you’re blaming Travis for [you should blame them, too] because they didn’t see it, either. I think that’s a charitable way of putting it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the firm said in a blog post.

Sources indicate that investors in the new round valued the tech giant at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage latest technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for latest conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Sources indicate that with the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is right now designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.
  • StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft.
  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a new round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

Industry observers note that stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The company has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

It has been revealed that “A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer stated an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

Sources indicate that it also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor said up to 5,000 consumers may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity claims it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

In a recent development, how it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

Industry observers note that more than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company indicates, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

Sources indicate that stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a firm’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-latest releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Recent findings suggest that along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

Sources indicate that stepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity notes its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

In a recent development, the tech giant has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

Industry observers note that what’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company says it also intends to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

#64647. Can AI Hack Smart Contracts? How AI Agents Are Changing Blockchain Security

Can AI Hack Smart Contracts? How AI Agents Are Changing Blockchain Security

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: U

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that smart contract vulnerability scanners typically work by looking for certain patterns.
  • Sources indicate that for example, in December 2025, Anthropic released results from SCONE-bench, a smart contract benchmark of 405 contracts that were exploited in the 2020 - 2025 period.
  • To make sure the agent was not simply memorising exploits that were already published, newer vulnerabilities that had been published after their training cutoff were tested on Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5, which were able to generate $4.6 million (simulated stolen funds).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that smart contract vulnerability scanners typically work by looking for certain patterns. However, because an AI agent can iterate and make use of dependencies, local blockchain forks, and decompilation, it weakens the protection gained by keeping source code secret, and can attempt attacks against complex vulnerabilities such as access control bugs, accounting errors, oracle-related bugs and unexpected contract interactions.

Sources indicate that for example, in December 2025, Anthropic released results from SCONE-bench, a smart contract benchmark of 405 contracts that were exploited in the 2020 - 2025 period. They were able to reproduce exploits for 207 contracts, totalling $550.1 million (simulated stolen funds).

To make sure the agent was not simply memorising exploits that were already published, newer vulnerabilities that had been published after their training cutoff were tested on Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5, which were able to generate $4.6 million (simulated stolen funds).

Finally, they analysed 2,849 recent smart contracts with no known concerns, discovering two previously unknown vulnerabilities that could have resulted in $3,694 (simulated stolen funds), emphasising the ability of AI agents to discover new vulnerabilities rather than simply exploiting known ones.

Anthropic emphasised that no actual funds were lost during these experiments. It should also be noted that in one of their experiments using GPT-5, it cost $3,476 for API usage, which leaves a slim (simulated) profit.

According to recent reports, with automated hacking becoming more effective, how can we be sure that DeFi will be able to stay ahead of these AI agents? Hacken, a blockchain security firm, reported that $1.18 billion was lost in 107 crypto hacks during the third quarter of 2026. 48% of this was from exploiting smart contracts.

Of course, this doesn’t specify the cause of these hacks. Regardless, it emphasises the importance of being able to stay ahead of AIs which could be used for exploitation.

Chainalysis estimates that approximately $36.7 million was stolen in 2026 from DeFi protocols that had not undergone smart contract verification. It also notes AI-assisted reverse engineering as an emerging risk without attributing any particular thefts to AI.

In an experiment by a16z on 20 past DeFi price manipulation exploits, apparent success rates of 50% were reduced to 10% when the researchers restricted access to transactional data that revealed the original exploit. When the researchers gave the AI some high-level information about the DeFi domain, success rates jumped to 70%.

In February 2026, OpenAI and Paradigm released a benchmark for evaluating agents’ abilities in the domains of vulnerability detection, patching, and exploitation using an EVM environment (EVMbench). Results revealed that GPT-5.3-Codex achieved a 71% success rate in exploitation (limited to a sandboxed environment) and 33.3% for GPT-5.

Recent findings suggest that in October 2026, CyberChainBench was released, analyzing 541 exploit events across 9 Ethereum-compatible blockchains. The best-performing configuration achieved 37.5%, 43.7%, and 23.4% success rates for detection, exploitation, and patching respectively.

In a simulation, the best-performing agent profited $57.4 million from exploits on 200 exploit events that occurred after the cutoff. Some of the reported high-severity challenges were evaluated and determined to not be exploitable by OpenZeppelin. Since much of the data is trained on in the public, results may be exaggerated.

Sources indicate that agents will continue to improve, and while current results are not an indication that AI-driven agents are responsible for large scale on-chain thefts, it is an indication that AI can find and exploit weaknesses in smart contracts given a certain environment. Given the ease with which agents can try attacking many different protocols, smaller protocols may see an uptick in exploit attempts.

Teams that implement rigorous testing and monitoring could have an edge over other teams. For example, AI could be used to test a contract prior to deployment, generate regression tests, and identify weird behavior on-chain. A human would still need to verify any potential issues and sign off on changes.

Teams should continue to perform third-party audits and implement other security best practices such as limiting access to sensitive information, setting up alerts and response looks, restricting the amount of money in a wallet, making sure AI systems do not have permissions to transact without human oversight where necessary, and so on.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.
  • On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding.
  • The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.

On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The organization’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a initiative that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.

The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal indicates the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.

Recent findings suggest that CEO Raj Aggarwal claims contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”.

In a recent development, supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, released by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

Sources indicate that as Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.

“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really massive impact.”.

5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Reflecting Sunlight From Space, Better Breathing And Smarter Garbage Trucks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar.
  • What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth?
  • Recent findings suggest that those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here.

What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car?

Recent findings suggest that those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a company bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a major business. Let’s take a closer look.

Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down.

According to recent reports, to that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant recently revealed $73.5 million in latest funding, bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase. Existing investors Sequoia Capital, Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures, Convective Capital, The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1.

In a recent development, reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be launched aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The company envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark.

The idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial rolls out, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships.

The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally, per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records.

Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade.

The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness manufacturer recently announced a $62 million investment from Camino Partners, the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky.

Intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It states it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years.

Sources indicate that intake prepares to use the new capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful.

Industry observers note that its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data shows.

In a recent development, interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026.

Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana, with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital, Harlem Capital and CreativeCo.

The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets.

Recent findings suggest that trashLab says its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection.

The tech giant indicates hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform.

It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot, a London-based organization using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026.

Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time.

Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler.

The startup recently unveiled a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator, Thin Line Capital, Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor.

Neuron is developing a newly introduced kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language.

According to recent reports, its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get fresh production lines up and running.

It has been revealed that the startup says it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It plans to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.

The investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026.

Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget.

Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros.

The Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital and EWOR, among other investors. The organization describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date.

Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions.

Industry observers note that customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth.

Unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite debuted in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch.

Tumbleweed claims its upcoming funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028.

Tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026, compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data demonstrates.

#64643. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1889 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

The disastrous enhancement that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

According to recent reports, no. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

Recent findings suggest that the question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the Latest York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella stated, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Industry observers note that full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a firm partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in significant, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

It has been revealed that since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Industry observers note that over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the firm with reports.

In a recent development, the first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

Industry observers note that no surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

It has been revealed that in theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple owners to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

Industry observers note that the cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to problem OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are vital enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security concern involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Sources indicate that nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he noted, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Sources indicate that here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

It has been revealed that managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

Sources indicate that it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

According to recent reports, it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data.
  • XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median.
  • XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data. The options market indicates that traders are now preparing for price swings that could be nearly double XRP's historical seven-day price move.

XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median. This figure far exceeds similar metrics for major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL).

XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility. Solana shows the lowest premium among these four cryptocurrencies, Coinbase remarked.

As the chart below indicates, the options-implied seven-day price move for XRP is around 9.6%, according to Glassnode and Coinbase data as of Nov. 17. This compares to its historical median absolute price move of about 4.9%.

Basically, this means that the options market is signaling a price swing nearly twice as large as XRP's typical seven-day price movement.

It has been revealed that interestingly, Solana's implied price move is also close to 9.5%, almost the same as XRP's. Yet its historical median weekly price move is much higher at about 6.5%.

The key here is that although both cryptocurrencies exhibit similarly large potential price moves, the magnitude of the expected volatility surprise is significantly greater for XRP relative to its usual trading range.

Recent findings suggest that for comparison, Bitcoin shows an options-implied seven-day move of about 6%, versus its historical median of about 3.5%. For Ethereum, these numbers are about 8% and 5.1%, respectively.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, this latest figure doesn't necessarily imply that XRP is going to crash. It's a sign that options traders expect a big price move regardless of its direction.

Implied volatility is a forward-looking measure. It's based on options prices. The higher the implied volatility, the more traders pay for exposure to potential price movements or protection against them.

Sources indicate that the chart from Coinbase is based on a one-standard-deviation estimate. It's derived by converting annualized at-the-money implied volatility into a seven-day timeframe.

For XRP, the roughly 9.6% implied move represents a statistical range. It's not a guaranteed price target. A one-standard-deviation range suggests about a 68% chance of the price staying within this range under typical modeling assumptions.

Thus, the latest figure of 1.94x implies that XRP's volatility premium remains high despite a slight decrease from the previous reading.

According to recent reports, from XRP traders' perspective, this can be a very challenging market environment. For traders using leverage, there could be a high risk of liquidation due to potentially sharp price moves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he indicates that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a latest sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”.

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

Sources indicate that the now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the tech giant has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

According to recent reports, could 2027 finally be the year Cardano (ADA) overtakes Ripple (XRP) in the cryptocurrency rankings? Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that, despite XRP’s established position among the industry’s largest digital assets, network upgrades, renewed institutional interest, and a shift in investor sentiment could make it more likely than it first appears.

Both cryptocurrencies have spent years competing for attention, albeit with very different propositions. XRP has built its reputation around cross-border payments and financial infrastructure, while Cardano has focused on research-driven development, decentralized applications, and a carefully structured ecosystem.

It has been revealed that however, market leadership can change swiftly during a cryptocurrency bull market. If Cardano delivers on its ambitious development roadmap while XRP struggles to maintain its momentum, the gap between the two could narrow considerably.

And while flipping XRP would require an extraordinary rally, ADA could climb to a valuation few investors presently anticipate.

One of Cardano’s biggest opportunities heading into 2027 is its ongoing push to improve network scalability.

The planned Ouroboros Leios upgrade is particularly key. Designed to increase transaction throughput without compromising Cardano’s decentralized architecture, Leios could address a longstanding criticism: its ability to compete with higher-throughput blockchain ecosystems.

It has been revealed that cardano’s Dijkstra development cycle also introduces further improvements, with Peras activation targeted for the second quarter of 2027. Peras is designed to improve transaction settlement speed by reducing the time needed to achieve stronger confirmation confidence.

Meanwhile, developments around programmable tokens, decentralized finance, and real-world asset tokenization could help Cardano attract applications that generate genuine demand for ADA.

These upgrades won’t automatically translate into higher token prices, but successful implementation could give investors a compelling reason to reconsider Cardano’s long-term valuation.

XRP has several advantages that Cardano cannot easily replicate. Ripple has spent years building relationships across the financial sector, while the XRP Ledger continues to expand into institutional decentralized finance, stablecoins, and tokenized real-world assets.

The network processed an average of approximately 2.48 million daily transactions during the first quarter of 2026, while its real-world asset market capitalization reached $2.25Bn. These are meaningful indicators of ecosystem activity.

However, XRP’s enormous market capitalization also creates a challenge for investors seeking outsized returns. With a much larger valuation than ADA, XRP needs substantially more capital inflows to achieve the same percentage gains.

Sources indicate that recent market comparisons have placed XRP’s valuation at roughly ten times Cardano’s, highlighting the scale of the challenge. If capital rotates toward smaller, established layer-1 networks during the next bull market, ADA could benefit disproportionately.

ADA previously reached an all-time high around $3.10 during the 2021 bull market, demonstrating that the cryptocurrency can attract substantial speculative demand when market conditions are favorable.

A sustained recovery towards its previous peak would be an crucial psychological milestone. However, a genuine breakout beyond that region would potentially open the door to a much larger valuation.

For XRP, the challenge is maintaining its market leadership while competing with an expanding range of payment-focused blockchain networks. Its established institutional presence provides a strong foundation, but continued adoption growth will be necessary to justify a substantially higher valuation.

The key technical signal to watch for ADA is a sustained sequence of higher highs and higher lows on the weekly and monthly charts, accompanied by improving relative strength against XRP.

A decisive break above previous cycle resistance, followed by a successful retest, could signal that a longer-term trend reversal is underway.

Consider an optimistic scenario in which the broader cryptocurrency market enters another substantial bull phase during 2027.

Cardano successfully implements its major upgrades, DeFi activity expands, institutional interest improves, and investors begin viewing ADA as an undervalued alternative to larger blockchain assets.

Under these circumstances, a move towards $1.50–$2.50 becomes an interesting longer-term price scenario, with the upper end representing a substantial recovery towards its previous all-time high.

At $2.50, Cardano’s market capitalization would approach $95 billion, assuming a circulating supply of approximately 38 billion ADA. That would represent a significant increase from its current valuation.

However, overtaking XRP would depend on more than Cardano’s own performance. XRP’s valuation would also need to be considered, meaning ADA could reach $2.50 without necessarily overtaking its rival.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that Cardano has a genuine opportunity to flip XRP in 2027, with ADA potentially reaching $2.50.

Although XRP remains the more established cryptocurrency, Meta AI believes Cardano offers the more interesting upside opportunity if its development roadmap translates into meaningful ecosystem growth.

Recent findings suggest that the deciding factor will be execution. If Leios, Peras, and Cardano’s broader adoption initiatives deliver, 2027 could be the year ADA finally challenges XRP’s dominance.

Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, slowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit.
  • Industry observers note that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge.
  • All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, slowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

Industry observers note that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

The reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery strategy has been confirmed.

According to recent reports, the design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

The Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most important fact is still missing. SlowMist says the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

It has been revealed that the lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. Users with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its initiative for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?
